subsubtopic: AID TO NEWFOUNDLAND UNDER DREE PROGRAM-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, 1 rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity under the provisions of Standing Order 43.
In view of the fact that, for the first time since the inception of DREE, Newfoundland does not have a forestry agreement with Ottawa, that the cash flow under DREE agreements with Newfoundland will decline from approximately $60 million a year to under $40 million during this year, that the Forestry 2 agreement, a land survey and mapping agreement, an amendment to the Nordco agreement and a new Nordco agreement have been ready for execution for months, with a coastal Labrador agreement pending as well, 1 move, seconded by the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander):
That the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion attend to urgent matters in his department, including correspondence and telexes from the premier of Newfoundland, and that the minister sign immediately the Forestry 2 agreement, the land survey and mapping agreement, the Nordco amendment and new Nordco agreement, and the coastal Labrador agreement so that work can commence in Newfoundland and Labrador under these agreements immediately, supplying needed facilities and creating needed employment.

subsubtopic: EASTERN PROVINCIAL AIRWAYS-ATLANTIC CANADA SERVICE-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
In light of the fact that the president of Eastern Provincial Airways has said that the airline may have to shut down some of its local routes, that the reason given was the Canadian Transport Commission's decision to extend CP Air's service to Halifax, that the former temporary prime minister and his party overwhelmingly supported CP Air's application to extend service to Halifax, and that these Atlantic communities depend on EPA's regional carrier service, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie):
That the Minister of Transport guarantee to the residents of Atlantic Canada the continuation of EPA's regional carrier service to all communities presently receiving these services, and that EPA be granted the Halifax-Toronto route instead of Canadian Pacific Airlines.

PROJECTS FOR EASTERN CANADA-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
Despite the government's admission of the danger of dependence upon foreign oil as the source of energy generation in east coast provinces, alternate energy projects like Cape Breton coal development and construction of the eastern extension of the natural gas pipeline are being delayed. I move, seconded by the hon. member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse):
That this House direct the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources to prepare and present immediately a plan to implement alternate energy projects in eastern Canada and include a schedule for the construction of the natural gas pipeline extension to reduce eastern Canada's dependence on foreign oil.

subsubtopic: DISPOSAL OF RADIOACTIVE WASTE-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity pursuant to the provisions of Standing Order 43.
In view of the decision yesterday by the British Columbia Supreme Court to award $458,700 damages to three firms in Surrey, British Columbia, who were deceived into buying radioactive waste while under the impression that it was land fill, and in light of the fact that the award was given because this material was considered harmful, yet more of this waste exists on other property in Surrey but cannot be removed because an appropriate disposal site has yet to be found, I
move, seconded by the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock-North Delta (Mr. Friesen):
That this House immediately authorize the Atomic Energy Control Board to remove this waste to the Atomic Energy of Canada Limited waste site at Chalk River.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
Recently, the government changed the requirements for fishermen receiving vessel subsidies from the federal government. Whereas it is now necessary for fishermen in western Canada to fill in a myriad of bureaucratic forms which previously were unnecessary, and whereas in light of these developments many fishermen in remote communities may be discouraged or prevented from purchasing new vessels, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Alberni (Mr. Miller):
That in the opinion of this House the government should take immediate steps to eliminate these needless bureaucratic requirements and to ensure that the procedures for necessary vessel subsidy will be the same as they were prior to the 1980 fiscal year.

subsubtopic: CALL FOR IMPROVED SUBURBAN SERVICE-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I also rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43. In view of locating postal lock-boxes as far as two blocks' distance away from a householder and calling this "suburban service" which is a misnomer of Orwellian proportions, and since older subdivisions receive doorstep letter carrier service while new residential areas are condemned to suburban service, and since awarding of an inferior service to one set of taxpayers and a superior one for their neighbours is unjust and discriminatory, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Hovdebo):
That this House urge the Postmaster General to halt the expansion of suburban service forthwith and to proceed with letter carrier delivery as rapidly as possible.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, 1 rise on a matter of urgent necessity concerning branches of the Canadian Legion in eastern Ontario and throughout Canada with regard to the proposed move of the Department of Veterans Affairs to Prince Edward Island announced a year ago by the Liberal government, which constitutes blatant political patronage that the Progressive Conservative administration was saddled with. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Darling):
In view of the objections of dozens of Canadian Legion branches across Canada to this completely unjustified action, that this House requests the government to immediately cancel all plans for the movement of DVA to Prince Edward Island, leaving the department where it now is and where it is better located to serve the veterans of this country.

subsubtopic: LANDED IMMIGRANT STATUS FOR MENNONITES-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to move a motion under the provisions of Standing Order 43. In view of the concern and sympathetic position which Canada has already taken toward refugees, as most recently demonstrated in the case of the Indo-Chinese refugees, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie):
That the Mennonite families of Canada who are now facing deportation, even though their parents were born in Canada and moved to Mexico, where these families were not informed of the regulation that they would have had to state their intention prior to their twenty-fourth birthday to remain Canadian citizens, be given the same consideration as other refugees and be granted Canadian landed immigrant status on compassionate grounds.

subsubtopic: TARIFF TO PROTECT BRITISH COLUMBIA POTATO GROWERS- MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity concerning the plight of potato producers in British Columbia.
In view of the fact that the actions of successive Liberal governments have virtually eliminated the french fried potato industry in British Columbia, thus destroying a major market for B.C. potatoes, and in view of the fact that potatoes imported from Washington state and Oregon are undermining Canadian producers by flooding the B.C. market with cheap potatoes from large factory farms, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Fraser Valley West (Mr. Wenman):
That the government move immediately to impose a seasonal tariff to protect British Columbia potato farmers from low-cost, imported spuds, by implementing the fast track method which was devised by the previous Progressive Conservative minister of agriculture and announced by him on October 22 of last year.

May 2, 1980

subtopic: COST OF IMPORTED OIL-SOURCE OF ADDITIONAL MONEYS
COST OF IMPORTED OIL-SOURCE OF ADDITIONAL MONEYS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have a question I would like to have addressed to the Minister of Finance. In his absence, I will direct it to whoever would presume to be the acting prime minister.
Given the notice by Saudi Arabia and Mexico in the last few days of their intention to significantly increase oil prices, and recognizing that this will immediately cancel out the $1 billion that we now understand the government has found a way to secure from the total oil dollar package, can the acting prime minister indicate to the House today where it is he intends to find and pay for this lost $1 billion which, of course, will result from the pending increases in oil that we will learn about on May 7 from OPEC?

subtopic: COST OF IMPORTED OIL-SOURCE OF ADDITIONAL MONEYS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I have been reflecting on and admiring the quality of the answer that was given by the Minister of State.

subtopic: COST OF IMPORTED OIL-SOURCE OF ADDITIONAL MONEYS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: COST OF IMPORTED OIL-SOURCE OF ADDITIONAL MONEYS
speechtext: One might refer to the fact that we had a discussion on that yesterday in this very House. A number of possibilities were indicated. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources-rightly, in my humble view-has repeatedly said that he is not going to comment on a daily basis on the consultations in which he is presently involved.

subtopic: COST OF IMPORTED OIL-SOURCE OF ADDITIONAL MONEYS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I do not know whether it occurs to the acting prime minister, humble though he would lead us to believe, that it is a fact that Atlantic Canada is dependent upon a significant amount of imported oil.
We would like to know from what source the government intends to raise the money to pay for this oil and thus enhance the possibility of secure oil supplies for that part of Canada. This is a very serious question. We now face a $4.3 billion oil compensation deficit. Where is the government going to get the money to pay for it? How can we in Atlantic Canada feel assured that we can afford to buy the imported oil that we require to sustain ourselves?

subtopic: COST OF IMPORTED OIL-SOURCE OF ADDITIONAL MONEYS
speechtext: 1 can understand the hon. member's curiosity, but the answer to his query will be given in due course.

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre Bussieres (Minister of State, Finance):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the hon. member knows quite well that all negotiations on the domestic oil price are under way, that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources has been doing considerable work in that field, that the Minister of Finance has begun a preliminary consideration of the next budget, taking into account those negotiations as well as their results in the preparation of that budget. The hon. member will then obtain a more explicit answer to his question.

Madam Speaker, I think I would prefer the "Stengelese" of the Minister of Transport, who in fact is the acting prime minister, to that kind of gobbledygook, because the question is very important.
I want to Find out from this government whether before the Minister of Energy embarked on his tour-for which we wish him well-as he visits the provinces, if advice given to him included advice to seek the support of the non-producing provinces for further increases in the total oil dollar that is now available. What I am seeking is information as to how the government intends to replace the $1 billion that has been wiped out in the last 24 hours.

Madam Speaker, I have a question which might have been directed to the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance, but since it involves general policy I will direct it to the acting prime minister.
The hon. gentleman is no doubt aware that the budget introduced in December, 1979, contained a special provision pertaining to Atlantic Canada's dependence on foreign oil as a source of electrical generation. Under this special provision, Nova Scotians would have been protected from additional costs of electrical generation caused by oil price increases through federal grants which would have exceeded, in total, $300 million.
Does the acting prime minister agree that such an assistance program is justified, and will he assure the House that his government will provide the same or a similar assistance program when his made-in-Canada price is established?

Madam Speaker, I will pass the question to the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance, and to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, but I cannot help underlining at this point that the record of the government in terms of protecting consumers, particularly in the importing provinces, is an exceptional one.

Hear, hear!
May 2, 1980

I appreciate the difficulties under which the acting prime minister operates in this field, but these are matters of great concern to the people of Atlantic Canada.
In Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island, the premiers have announced that if this program of assistance is continued, the price of electrical energy can be maintained in 1980 and 1981 despite increases in the price of oil. I should like to know whether the acting prime minister, or anybody else on the government side, can assure us that this assistance will be continued and that electrical prices will not be increased, as they would not have been increased under the Progressive Conservative budget.
Because of his very special interest in that area, the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance will obviously bear that in mind when he prepares his budget.

subsubtopic: ACTION TO SOLVE PROBLEMS OF RENTERS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is addressed to the minister responsible for CMHC. Since Canada is suffering the most serious housing shortage in recent history, with a drop of 17 per cent in housing starts predicted for 1980, and since those who are suffering most are tenants who will never be able to own a home, will the minister tell us what action he intends to take to solve this housing problem, particularly in regard to renters who are paying well over 30 per cent of their incomes for shelter?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul J. Cosgrove (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
subsubtopic: ACTION TO SOLVE PROBLEMS OF RENTERS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I had the opportunity, at the beginning of this week, of speaking to the minister responsible for housing in the province of British Columbia and assessing at first-hand some of the problems in the riding of the hon. member who raised this question.
I certainly share her concern. I intend to speak with all the provincial ministers with whom 1 have not yet spoken, and I can assure the hon. member that the question of the supply of rental accommodation is high on the priority list of both my department and of the corporation.

subsubtopic: ACTION TO SOLVE PROBLEMS OF RENTERS
speechtext:
I appreciate that the minister was in British Columbia and listening intently to the concerns of the west last weekend, with no commitments being made. However, his own CMHC report shows that Vancouver has the worst housing crisis in North America, and that cities like Calgary and Victoria are not far behind. In Vancouver, over a quarter of the population has housing problems: some 11,000 people, for example, have inadequate housing and there is a minus zero vacancy rate and a migration of 25,000 to that region.
Oral Questions
Will the minister be specific and tell us what measures he plans to take to alleviate these problems in cities which are suffering from huge migration?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
subsubtopic: ACTION TO SOLVE PROBLEMS OF RENTERS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as I indicated, the problem is not necessarily one which can be addressed by the federal government or by the corporation itself. The whole question of housing, as hon. members can well appreciate, is one which involves many jurisdictions. For example, I am heartened to see that in the province of Alberta this week, that province redirected $60 million from its surplus toward addressing problems in some of the tight market areas there.
As I indicated-and I will repeat it- I am working with the ministers from the provinces. I hope there will be a federal response, but the response will be one in co-operation with the provinces.

subsubtopic: SAFETY OF PERSONS LIVING IN PROXIMITY OF PENITENTIARIES
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Solicitor General. In view of the murder of a local citizen, allegedly by an inmate from the Mountain prison in British Columbia, can the minister advise this House and the community what measures or changes in policy he is contemplating to ensure the safety of the residents of that area?

subsubtopic: SAFETY OF PERSONS LIVING IN PROXIMITY OF PENITENTIARIES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, 1 have asked for a report on that particular incident, but I have learned in the meantime that the Mountain penitentiary has only a single fence around it to protect it. Double fence was intended to be built, but it had been delayed because of a decision about construction inside the yard. I have ordered a second fence to be built, and that is currently being built.
In view of the incident referred to, that news is small comfort but, as hon. members will be aware, the escaped inmate has been captured by the RCM Police.

subsubtopic: SAFETY OF PERSONS LIVING IN PROXIMITY OF PENITENTIARIES
speechtext: And he will be out on the weekend with a pass.

subsubtopic: SAFETY OF PERSONS LIVING IN PROXIMITY OF PENITENTIARIES
speechtext: Considering the series of incidents involving inmates from penal institutions in the Abbotsford-Matsqui area, including the abduction and murder of a female employee of an all-night store, allegedly by an inmate, has the minister ordered a full inquiry into all these incidents in order that the legitimate fears and growing resentments of the communities may be allayed, and confidence in the Canadian penitentiary service restored ?

subsubtopic: SAFETY OF PERSONS LIVING IN PROXIMITY OF PENITENTIARIES
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I would agree with the hon. member if there had been an increase in the rate of escapes across the country or in any particular region. That is not the case. 1 am still concerned about every incident and, as hon. members know, I have received a report on each of the escapes. However, I do not think the situation justifies a general investigation of the problem which is no more serious now than it has been in the past. I am approaching them on a case-by-case basis.

speechtext:
I rise on a question of privilege. Madam Speaker. The Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) has implied that the delay in the approval of Summer Youth Employment projects is because of the failure of New Democratic Party members of Parliament to take their responsibilities seriously vis-a-vis the minister's recommendations that members submit indications of which projects in their ridings they would deem worthy of funding.
The minister knows full well that members of this party are not in a position where they have delayed approval of projects, but they have made representations to the minister that he change the way in which approval is given for funding. The minister asked that there be input from members of Parliament as to which projects should be worthy of funding, but did not, on the one hand, give members any final say so that they would be responsible for the input they gave into the funding process, nor, on the other hand, did he make provision for any sort of community input.
We made representations to the minister that if he was willing to set up a community participation process for input, if he was willing to set up committees at the community level, we would be willing to go ahead with that.
This would have been consistent with all the rhetoric about community participation that the Minister of Employment and Immigration was so fond of indulging in prior to his election to government.
We did send in our forms and we indicated to the minister what our position was on this. There is no way that our actions have in any way delayed approval of these projects; if anything, they should have speeded it up because he did not have to go through the process of sorting out what the input of the various members of Parliament was with regard to projects in our ridings.
The implication of what the minister said with regard to our carrying out our responsibilities is wrong. It misleads the people of Manitoba, it misleads this House, and it does not do justice to the facts. I submit this should be regarded as a question of privilege. Madam Speaker.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in all honesty, I think the hon. member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie) may have a certain difference of opinion, but he certainly does not have a question of privilege. I would just like to point out to him certain facts that would support my case.
The first is that when this government took office the procedure by which consultation would take place on a local level through members of Parliament had been totally cancelled. The previous government had decided for its own reasons not to allow any form of consultation on the local level. At that point the Summer Youth Employment program was already in progress. The announcements had already been
May 2, 1980

made, the advertisements had already gone out and applications were already being submitted.
It was our feeling, based upon a very strong commitment to the notion, that before deciding on Summer Youth Employment programs there should be some avenue by which the local community is represented and priorities judged. The best way to do that is to consult with the member of Parliament concerned. It may be that the hon. member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill does not have the same respect for the role of the member of Parliament as we on this side.
I should like to point out that one of the reasons a person is elected is to speak for his or her community. There was certainly no prohibition whatsoever in the instructions or information we sent out that would have prevented the hon. member or any of his colleagues from consulting with groups in his own community in order to set up whatever form of procedure he wanted to follow.
I should also like to point out that the matter only came to my attention in a letter that I received, I believe yesterday or it may have been the day before, from the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow), indicating that members of the New Democratic Party caucus were not going to participate in that consultative feature.
Where the delay occurred was simply that we were waiting for them to come in. It is certainly their right if they do not want to participate or give advice and there is no compulsion for them to do so; but we were waiting for those applications. Now that we know they are not going to submit them, we will proceed with the evaluation and assessment without that kind of input.
As I say, Madam Speaker, it is their right to do that and I was not suggesting they were doing anything wrong. But the procedure was set up and we were only informed a few days ago that they would not be participating.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. Gilles Lamontagne (Minister of National Defence):
subsubtopic: TABLING OF FINAL REPORT OF TASK FORCE ON UNIFICATION OF ARMED FORCES
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I have the honour of tabling in the House, pursuant to Standing Order 41(2), in both official languages, the final report of the Task Force on Unification of Armed Forces of Canada.
MR. MCKINNON-LACK OF opportunity to debate task FORCE REPORT ON UNIFICATION OF ARMED FORCES

Madam Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege concerning the document which the minister has just tabled. The practice of never hearing a statement on motions from a minister is infringing upon the privileges of members of this House. This particular minister has managed to choose a new fighter aircraft and has signed the largest contract ever signed in Canada without a statement on motions or giving members an opportunity to discuss the matter. Now we have this very important report commissioned by the former administration submitted to this minister six weeks ago tabled without comment.
This report is of great interest to the people of Canada, to the people in the armed forces and to this House. If we are not going to be given an opportunity to understand the government's position on this report, then the normal debate that is so healthy for our democracy is going to cease happening here. What we get are press releases and it is most difficult to debate things through a press release issued by the minister somewhere, some time and replied to somewhere, some time, by the opposition.
I would like to point out that the minister, who unfortunately left the House when I rose, would have had an opportunity to indicate the government's position on this report in reply to my raising this question of privilege. There are some 30 recommendations in the report. Perhaps he could say whether he accepts half of them or all of them or when he is going to accept them. At the very least he could have said he would refer it to the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence for consideration.
If the important business of the government is going to be conducted in this clandestine manner without public debate in this chamber, I feel that it infringes upon the privileges of all members and of Canadians.
[ Translation]

speakeroldname: Hon. Yvon Pinard (President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, because of the intervention of the hon. member, I think it is important to define a few things at this point. All of this is covered in our standing orders. What the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Lamontagne) has just done is to make public and table a report. Nothing forces him to make a statement. Standing Order 15(3) stipulates that a minister "may", in French the word is peul, make a statement or announcement. The Minister of National Defence chose not to make one today. It is his privilege, his right to so choose; it is quite in order for him to do so.
The colleague who rose on a question of privilege, which it really is not, will have many opportunities of putting questions to the Minister of National Defence. He can do so during the oral question period that will follow tabling of this report, and
May 2, 1980

also in committee when the estimates come up for study. Moreover, between now and December 10, the opposition will have 18 days allotted to them for the discussion of the topics of their choosing. In light of this, it is unfair to claim that the opposition is being deprived of the opportunity to discuss the report tabled today by the Minister of National Defence. On the contrary! All that is in the standing orders: As a matter of fact, they are most generous and provide the hon. member and his colleagues with ample opportunities to put questions and debate the subject dealt with in the report the Minister of National Defence tabled today. In closing, Madam Speaker, this is definitely not a matter of privilege and I think hon. members should see to it that this procedure of bringing up questions of privilege should be not be abused lest it no longer be taken seriously.
It may happen on occasion that hon. members' rights are really infringed upon. I would hate to see the day-because hon. members are developing the habit of getting into all sorts of political argument under the guise of questions of privilege-when our rights are really infringed upon and the question of privilege be ruled out of order because abuse will have been too obvious in the past.

Madam Speaker, 1 feel that I must object to what was an extraordinary statement made by the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Pinard) and government House leader. He stated in essence that members of his government feel obliged to cater to the democratic responsibilities of this institution only when the rules specifically demand them; otherwise we can resort to press releases and that type of debate. That is absolutely unacceptable and it certainly infringes on the privileges of the entire nation as well as members of this House.

Madam Speaker, I rise on the same question of privilege. I find myself in the unusual position of agreeing with two speakers from the Conservative party on this question of privilege. In both instances in the last few weeks that the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Lamontagne) has brought forward two very important positions on national defence, they have not been brought before the House. We are in a position right now where there are some very important questions to be answered with regard to the future of our armed forces, and the minister brings them in, tables them and does not allow us to debate the matter in this House.
The President of the Privy Council (Mr. Pinard) said that we are raising these questions of privilege so often that they will not be taken seriously. 1 submit that by the type of action the Minister of National Defence has carried on in the last few weeks, Parliament will not be taken seriously in the future if we are not allowed to debate important issues, issues that will make a major difference to our armed forces in the future.
Introduction of Bills
There are some very important questions asked in this task force report. These are questions that must be answered very soon. Members of this House as the representatives of the people of Canada must be allowed to debate these questions and try and find some good solutions and answers to the problems. I urge that this question of privilege be upheld, that the minister make a statement and that we be allowed to question him on it.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The rules are quite clear. They stipulate that the minister may make a statement when he is tabling documents. That has to mean that he may decide not to make a statement when tabling documents, if he so chooses. That may be wise or unwise; it is not for the Chair to decide. The Chair cannot force a minister to make a statement when tabling a document.

speechtext:
May I refer at this point to the balloting practice which has been followed to determine the precedence for the introduction and first reading of Private Members' Public Bills. On today's order paper there are listed some 395 bills standing in the name of various hon. members.
It was not practical or possible for the Chair to review the provisions of each of those bills. Might I therefore suggest to the House that we adopt the procedure which was agreed upon in the past several sessions; namely, that we proceed to the introduction, first reading and orders for the printing of these bills so that each may be scrutinized between now and its being called for second reading in order to allow the Chair to consider whether there is any defect in the bills itLrespect of the practices and usages of the House.
I suggest that, by unanimous consent, all the Private Members' Public Bills listed for introduction on today's order paper be deemed to have been introduced, given first reading, ordered to be printed and to stand for second reading at the next sitting of the House, subject, as always, to a subsequent examination as to the regularity of each bill.
In order to ensure that bills at the top of the list will not have to stand because they have not been printed and distributed when called, I am requesting the Deputy Speaker, with the co-operation of the Table officers, to give the necessary instructions to ensure that printing and distribution priorities will reflect the order determined in the draw and, to that effect, the word "printed" will be added to the order paper entry for each bill when received by the distribution branch.
Is the procedure to which I have referred agreed to by the House?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean-Luc Pepin (Minister of Transport) moved
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO IMPROVE PUBLIC SAFETY
speechtext:
that Bill C-18, to promote public safety in the transportation of dangerous goods, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Transport.
He said: For the fourth time in two years, Madam Speaker, a government is calling upon Parliament to adopt transportation of dangerous goods legislation. The Hon. Otto Lang, the then minister of transport, introduced Bills C-53 and C-17 in May and November 1978, respectively. In turn, my immediate predecessor, the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankow-ski) introduced Bill C-25 in November 1979. These three bills, namely, Bills C-53, C-17 and C-25, have fallen victims to the parliamentary timetable.
As I refer to two previous attempts at legislating this increasingly important issue, I cannot gloss over hon. Jean Marchand's contribution. In 1973, he is the one who, as minister of transport, took upon himself to consult the various provincial governments for the purpose of streamlining their respective legislation and regulations concerning the highway transportation of dangerous goods. He is also the one who set up an interdepartmental committee to scrutinize the federal government's legislation and regulations concerning the transportation of goods.

May 2, 1980
Transportation of Dangerous Goods
[English)
Mr. Speaker, while it is unfortunate that this legislation should have been delayed so long, I believe that each return to square one has resulted in an improved bill. Indeed, each new version has received amendments incorporating suggestions found in submissions and comments made by industry and by provincial governments on the previous attempt. 1 will identify in committee only, because this is highly technical, the changes in Bill C-18 as compared with the former Bill C-25. On the other hand, other suggestions from industry have not been adopted and I will give reasons for rejecting them, again in the committee.
Another benefit derived from postponement is that more time has been available for informal consultation, particularly with industry, with respect to the development of the regulations which will be promulgated under this legislation. Finally in these introductory remarks-I should have said remarks introductory to my introductory remarks-in the time since the first proposal concerning the transportation of dangerous goods was submitted to this House, a number of accidents involving dangerous goods in transit has focused public attention on the subject. 1 consequently believe that growing public awareness of such risks will result in increased popular support for this legislation.
Needless to say, Mr. Speaker, 1 am pleased to be the "minister most likely to succeed" in getting this legislation on to the statute books, because 1 intend to make safety one of my main preoccupations during my tenure at Transport Canada.
This is not an easy bill, Mr. Speaker. My reading of the proceedings of the previous committee persuaded me there was a great deal of frustration among members of that committee. The very breadth of the subject matter is one of the causes of that frustration. The concept of umbrella legislation is another, because it involves to a great extent the acceptance of much of the status quo as opposed to the entire fresh look which one sometimes finds in legislation. Indeed, in desperation, one of the members of the committee suggested that Bill C-25, the bill which preceded the one in front of us now, was a "do nothing bill" and some members of the public have made the same allegation. Well, then, what is Bill C-18 all about?

Let us look first at the situation as it exists now in this field of transportation of dangerous goods. At the federal level, we find all sorts of legislation-the Railway Act, the Aeronautics Act, the Canada Shipping Act, the Nuclear Liability Act, the Oil and Gas Production and Conservation Act, the national ports and harbours bill, the Explosives Act, the Fertilizers Act and so on-a whole series of more or less specialized legislation dealing with particular goods or with general areas.
At the provincial level, we also find a variety of legislation. The Ontario gasoline handling act, the Quebec explosives act, legislation on pressurized containers, prevention and many others, of course.
At the municipal level also, there has been a growing awareness of the risks to public safety caused by the transportation of dangerous goods in urban areas. That led, for example, to the drafting of municipal bylaws dealing with zoning and the transportation of those products. A number of selfregulating bodies-for example those responsible for the operation of bridges, tunnels, canals-are imposing conditions on the transportation of dangerous goods in or on such facilities.
So there is a considerable number of very varied legislation and regulations involving various penalties at the three levels of government.
Now, from a practical point of view, that leads to a lot of confusion and conflicts. I have here a paper from my department commenting on that. It reads, and I quote:
Manufacturers, distributors and transporters of dangerous goods and their containers must sometimes ignore regulations or in certain circumstances contravene them directly to ensure the movement of those commodities.
The paper goes on to say:
There is no harmony between policies and enforcement authority, and the strict implementation of existing regulations not only does not ensure security but in certain cases could worsen the damages that could be caused by an accident.
So the point I want to make here is that such an accumulation of unco-ordinated legislation generates untold difficulties for transporters and adversely affects the domestic and international trade of this country.

This confusion is an obvious one. 1 want to emphasize the confusing maze of regulation varying, according to the means of transport being used, the substance being shipped and the places to or from which the goods are being carried.
Now, Mr. Speaker, believing, unlike Hamlet, that it is nobler in the mind to take up arms against a sea of troubles and by opposing end them, my predecessors in Transport Canada and I found ourselves faced with three possible options. This is really the gist of the matter.
The first option would have been to issue a code to be adopted and enforced by agencies at the federal or at the provincial level, using their own laws and regulations. The government would have issued such a code in the hope that authorities-federal, provincial and municipal-would incorporate these standards in their legislation or regulations.
As a second option, we could through some constitutional means have totally pre-empted the field, rendered all existing laws invalid and introduced a single piece of federal legislation. That would have been a federal takeover of the area using some general power that the federal government has or some emergency power, whatever it is. So that would have been the second way of going at it.
A third way is to adopt a sufficiently broad umbrella legislation which will provide a focus for co-ordinated activity. All my predecessors, and I today, have chosen this third avenue as being the best of three very difficult options.
May 2, 1980

Clearly, a code of standards would be unlikely to result in uniform regulations or regulations that could be enforced uniformly, since the powers conferred by the various statutes to the implementing agencies are unequal. So are the penalties. In other words, this code would have been implemented differently by different orders of government or under different bills, and in some ways while it might have resulted in some relative progress, it might also have added to the confusion that presently exists. So that was not too good as an option.
The second, the pre-emptive act, would have occasioned a major disruption in the administration, for one thing, because all these agencies would now have been superseded by legislation and, presumably, by an organization of some kind which would have taken over all these responsibilities. Not terribly good either.
Another reason is, of course, the constitutional issue. Each person arrested or sentenced under this pre-emptive law could have claimed that the bill was unconstitutional. He would have taken any number of appeals, going right up to the Supreme Court of Canada. Lawyers would have been very busy, but transportation would not have been helped very much.
The third option is the one which was selected by my predecessors and which is selected now. It is the typical Canadian compromise. It offers an umbrella type of law, an umbrella under which we find a number of basic principles and references to other laws and regulations, trying to incorporate most of it. It is not an easy matter to handle. That is why so much co-operation will be needed on the part of federal and provincial agencies in order to bring the maximum degree of uniformity to this area of regulation governing the transportation of dangerous goods.
I have read the bill a number of times and I, too, find it frustrating. This is why the committee will have to accept the frustration and move as well as it can to get the best common denominator.
I was speaking to a friend the other day. Jean Paul Sartre has just died. As we know, he was the grandfather of existentialism. I referred to this bill as an existentialist one. It will be in constant devenir. It will be in constant fabrication in some ways. One does not go to school for so long in his life without wanting others to know about it at one point, and this, presumably, is what I am doing now. I just want to emphasize that there is really, in my view, no other way of going at it.

Mr. Speaker, I simply want to give a few basic elements on the contents of Bill C-18, for the benefit of those who are going to read my remarks. As I indicated, the objective is very simple. It is to establish a single legislation under which existing agencies, whether federal or provincial, can apply everywhere in Canada a set of regulations governing standards, procedures and labelling for the handling of dangerous goods by any means of transport.
This bill is an effort to consolidate existing regulations. The
legislation establishes three new types of offence. First, the
Transportation of Dangerous Goods handling, the offer to transport or the transport of dangerous goods which do not comply with the regulations. This is the first offence. The second offence relates to packaging and labelling of dangerous goods which do not comply with the regulations.
A third offence concerns non-compliance with orders given by the minister or his agent in emergency situations.
The bill also provides for the appointment of inspectors who will be authorized to visit the premises, to inspect the goods, the packaging, the means of transport, the facilities and the warehouses, to take any measure deemed necessary or to request that such measures be taken, including the seizure, the removal and the destruction of dangerous products or goods and the evacuation of persons. Of course, these inspectors will also be able to issue tickets and deliver them to the offenders. However, once again, in most cases these inspectors will be those of the agencies already in existence at the various government levels. There is no question of creating a completely new inspection system for the administration of this act. The cost of this would obviously be prohibitive.
The bill also provides that inspectors and others will be able to take corrective action whenever there is an accident involving dangerous goods; it also provides a strict obligation concerning the expenses incurred by Her Majesty in right of Canada to prevent, remedy or repair any resulting damage. In other words, if an offender did not take preventive action before an accident occurs and Her Majesty is forced to repair the damages, Her Majesty will have a right of recourse against this offender. The bill also provides for inquiries to be made in all cases of accidents or incidents involving dangerous goods which have resulted in death or damage to property or the environment.
The minister or his agent can also issue orders to deem foreign standards equivalent or publish decrees in the areas where there are no general standards in Canada. In this way, we can simply adopt the measures which exist elsewhere in the world to use them internally.
The minister can also require information on the chemical composition of goods to determine first aid care to be given in an emergency. Everyone knows what this means. Some of these goods technically involve commercial secrets and if there is an accident, the minister will have the right to ask for the formula to determine the care to be given.

A few more pages, Mr. Speaker, a few words on the subject of regulations, a very popular subject in the last committee.
As I explained at the outset, the range and variety of the regulations attached to existing legislation is enormous. At the instigation of Senator Marchand, to whom I referred a moment ago, an interdepartmental committee was established to attempt to harmonize the regulations during the normal process of keeping them up to date. This exercise was frustrated by traditional practices in the industries affected and by the

May 2, 1980
Transportation of Dangerous Goods diversity of the various enabling acts. I hope 1 have at least given a clear impression of the diversity, variety and amplitude of the regulations existing in this area. 1 am trying to create a psychological climate. Much as we want to improve that situation, we have to be very realistic and know that progress will take time. Listening to us, and seeing us work in the committee, as we will, the public must not be possessed by aspirations and expectations which are immensely beyond the capacity of that law.
I am just trying to build a good amount of realism into this so that members of the committee and the public at large will know that, while progress can be made if there is a great amount of co-ordination, there are also a number of principles and rules which have to be firmly established. It will take years before we get the optimum result in this area. That is the practice of the art of the possible; that is what politics is all about.
Just over two years ago, in anticipation of this new legislation the Department of Transport issued a rough draft of the amalgamated regulations. Industrial associations were invited to comment, and since then two more drafts have been produced and circulated. Because of the need to identify some 3,000 individual substances and to regulate the design and construction of packaging containers and transport vehicles in which these products may be carried, the regulations appear bulky. In fact, they are less than half the number of regulations that now apply to the transportation of dangerous goods. A good deal of streamlining has taken place.
1 have one more remark which 1 must make at this point. It is with reference to Mr. Justice Samuel Grange who, as hon. members are aware, is conducting an inquiry into the railway accident which occurred at Mississauga last November. A copy of Bill C-18 has been sent to commissioner Grange and 1 have requested that he provide us with comments on it to the extent that he sees fit to do so.
It is not the commissioner's mandate to examine Bill C-18, but I hope that as a result of his inquiry into the cause of the accident at Mississauga and the adequacy of existing railway regulations, he may have some suggestions to make about the bill, particularly concerning the regulation-making powers and the regulations themselves. Any comments that Mr. Justice Grange makes in his final report, which is expected in September, concerning regulatory reform will, of course, be available to the Standing Committee on Transport.
I want to urge hon. members not to consider delaying consideration of this bill until the report is tabled. Again this is a question of practicality. It is unfortunately to be expected that following the Grange report there will be other accidents and other inquiries, and if we decide to wait until we have all the inquiries made available to us as a committee, the certainty exists that we will never pass a bill. So again 1 think we must be very practical and, as far as possible, invite Mr. Justice Grange to the committee hearings and not wait until we get his full report in September before we move.
Finally, my predecessor once removed said that he was tackling this job with an open mind. 1 want to say that my mind is as open as his and that in working all together we might achieve a bill which will be the beginning of great things.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not very often that one has the opportunity of making three speeches on the second reading of a bill in this chamber. I am in that rather unique position inasmuch as this is the third time that 1 have participated in the second reading debate on a bill entitled the transportation of dangerous goods act. As the minister has indicated, this bill has been before the House on three different occasions, and perhaps even on four.
Bill C-53 was introduced in May of 1978 and was never debated; it died on the order paper. It was repeated in the form of Bill C-17, which, I believe, was essentially the same. That was introduced in November, 1978, debated for about 20 or 30 minutes one Friday afternoon in February, and did not proceed beyond the half hour debate which took place in this House.
I believe it is important to lay that groundwork because, while this particular piece of legislation is important and while there was a considerable demand for it, it was not proceeded with immediately. As a matter of fact, I said at the time, and I have said this before, that during those days it was used more or less as a piece of legislation to fill out the activities of a Friday afternoon. The previous minister of transport on that occasion was not even in the House at the time second reading debate on that bill was introduced, so there was not a great deal of urgency attached to it at that time.
However, as the minister has indicated, the call for this kind of legislation has intensified rather dramatically, both from provincial and municipal levels of government as well as from the citizenry at large. As he has indicated as well, there have been a number of accidents. I can well appreciate what the minister said when he pointed out that trying to put together a piece of legislation which would co-ordinate all the rules and regulations and provide the necessary uniformity which could be understood and respected at all levels is a truly tangled web.
I can say to the House and to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) that our government recognized the importance of this legislation. We recognized that, given the complexity of the situation, it required intensive consultations and discussions with the provinces, with municipalities and indeed with the industry because, if this bid is to work, it must have the co-operation of all levels of government.
It must also have the respect and the understanding of the industry because, as I said, I believe, when I introduced the former Bill C-25 last November, it provides for inspectors; but we cannot have an inspector in every trailer or every train, so there has to be that kind of an understanding. As has been alluded to by the minister, the bill that we introduced was an improvement over the previous one. I agree with him when he used the phrase "constant fabrication". I am sure that this kind of legislation will evolve because in many cases we are
May 2, 1980

breaking new ground and it is undoubtedly true that we all want the most effective instrument possible to do the job.
We commenced the review of the previous Bill C-17 immediately after we assumed office in early June and recognized that the effectiveness of that bill would only come about with the co-operation of the provinces and the understanding of the industry. We recognized very quickly that if this legislation was to be successful, we could not take unilateral action but rather should move in a co-operative fashion.
Our bill was restructured rather extensively, but the objectives remained the same. We feel that essentially we strengthened the bill in some areas, and we have felt that some of the federal-provincial issues were clarified, we had hoped in the spirit of promoting greater understanding and respect for the legislation. Also we wanted to relieve somewhat the regulatory burden imposed upon the industry itself. 1 am sure that these discussions have been going on since this our bill was introduced and since it died on the order paper. I suggest that discussions should continue even though this bill might very well pass into law in this Parliament.
I should like to pay tribute to and commend the former minister of transport, now in the other place, who set up the mechanism for developing the necessary framework to proceed with this bill. I think it required a lot of patience. I am sorry that the bill did not become law when we introduced it on November 19. It was given second reading on November 27 and it was our intention to enshrine the previous Bill C-25 in our law books in early January, because at that time there was some sense of urgency.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a matter of fact I have not really made that conversion in total, but I will have no trouble referring to Your Honour as Mr. Speaker.
Also I should like to point out that I am very pleased the hon. member for Sarnia (Mr. Cullen) is in the House this
Transportation of Dangerous Goods
afternoon, because he too had a role to play in the facilitation of the passage of legislation dealing with the transportation of dangerous goods, inasmuch as it was he who introduced the previous Bill C-17 on Friday, February 16, 1979. I had the opportunity of responding to his intervention at that time. As I pointed out for the benefit of hon. members earlier, this is the third occasion on which I have intervened on second reading of this kind of bill to enact a transportation of dangerous goods act.
Prior to the adjournment I had indicated that our government introduced Bill C-25 on November 19, 1979. Second reading took place on November 27, 1979, and the bill had been passed on to committee. It was our intention that this bill be passed into law in early January. At that time there was a great sense of urgency about the passage of this legislation.
The opposition NDP-Liberal alliance were huffing and puffing for legislative action which had arisen largely as a result of the misfortune that occurred at Mississauga. We responded at that time with our bill. At the time the House of Commons became infiltrated with instant experts in all sorts of areas related to the transportation of dangerous goods. There were all sorts of charges and countercharges. Our government responded shortly thereafter by introducing our bill. The accident had occurred either on November 11 or November 12. We responded and the opposition stonewalled once we got into committee. There were all sorts of objections. They wanted to see regulations. They introduced all kinds of committee manoeuvres and tactics to see that the bill did not proceed.
The Minister of Transport has talked about realism, and I agree with the minister. He was not involved in the committee at that time, but I am sure that he has looked at the committee proceedings, and noticed that there was not a heck of a lot of realism among the NDP and Liberal members on that committee. There were such charges as, for instance, cutbacks in the CTC and cutbacks in safety inspectors.
Just to set the record straight, the initiative of any cutbacks within the CTC was taken by the formal Liberal administration. There were some 100 person-years to be reduced, it was up to the discretion of the CTC the president of the CTC to determine where those cutbacks should take place. It was up to him to determine if they would be at the administrative level, the secondary level or within the safety inspector services. That was a decision which was made by the CTC, and that charge cannot be accurately laid at our government's feet.
The stonewalling also consisted of a demand to see the regulations, which included some 1200 pages. I defy any member of this House to understand such a volume with any degree of expertise. We introduced the regulations. It was one of the first occasions in the history of parliamentary procedure in this country wherein the regulations were submitted to the committee for consideration at the same time as the bill was under consideration. That was the kind of co-operation and response which this government undertook to alleviate a very urgent and pressing situation. We gave the committee what

May 2, 1980
Transportation of Dangerous Goods they wanted, we extended the committee sittings, but the forces of the NDP and Liberal holy alliance played politics and stonewalled. As a result of those manoeuvres, the legislation is not in effect today. Those two parties huffed and puffed about all sorts of things.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO IMPROVE PUBLIC SAFETY
speechtext: Let's get on with it then.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO IMPROVE PUBLIC SAFETY
speechtext:
The hon. member says "Let's get on with it". That is precisely what we intend to do. We will not stonewall, and I give the Minister of Transport and the hon. member that commitment. This legislation is needed very badly.
1 am amazed at the cynicism and irresponsibility of some of the hon. members who served on that committee, not for the purpose of moving the bill and passing it into law, but for the purpose of playing politics and scoring political points. Like many other measures introduced by our government, this measure was deferred and delayed indefinitely. Some of our other good measures have been cancelled completely. Of course, Mr. Speaker, I am not directing my remarks to the Minister of Transport; he was not involved at the time, nor did he participate.
It is not my intention to review this matter unduly because it is political history, but those members who are responsible 1 hope will reflect on their performance. I am sure that they will recognize that they probably acted in bad faith and not in a spirit consistent with parliamentary democracy.
I believe that this bill should be dealt with in the most non-partisan fashion possible. I refer to the incidents which I have mentioned only because they did occur. It is not because there was a basic objection to the bill or because there was disagreement with the principles of the bill, but because some members wanted to participate in political gamesmanship.
We on this side support the principal objectives of this bill. The bill has the same objectives as the previous bills, and I do not wish to go into detail. The minister has pointed out the number of areas in which changes have been made. I am sure that those changes have been made for the better and will serve to strengthen and provide a more effective piece of legislation. That is good. This Parliament should demand the most effective piece of legislation possible because our citizens demand it.
I submit, as the minister has indicated, that this legislation will probably evolve, because of the kind of flexibility incorporated into this bill which will allow changes and amendments to take place from time to time, into a solid piece of legislation. I am sure that, on the basis of experience, many good recommendations and suggestions will flow from the Grange report which the minister will table, and I am particularly pleased that the minister has indicated that he welcomes any suggestions submitted to him by the Grange commission.
1 agree with the minister that it is not necessary to delay the passage of this bill when there are the necessary provisions to incorporate further changes to the bill including any further recommendations. Naturally, based upon previous experience of the administration of this bill, undoubtedly there will be a demand for changes and modifications to the regulations and to certain specific provisions of this piece of legislation.
Reference has been made to the regulations. Surely the regulations are the core of this bill. What we have in terms of the legislative framework are not simply the principles but the real heart and core of the bill. The bill's provisions are very complex and technical in nature, but I would hope that during the committee proceedings we will have an opportunity to hear an overview of the latest version of the regulations in the clearest form possible.
1 understand that there have been continuing consultations with the provinces and industry with respect to the development of the best set of regulations that can be utilized and implemented. We would like to have an opportunity to look at these recommendations and to deal with them to ensure, in a parliamentary and official sense, that those who may have some reservations or concerns about any part of the bill will have the opportunity to express their views in committee.
We will also want to invite witnesses to participate in the further discussion of this legislation. It is not our intention to delay unduly passage of the bill as it seems to have been around for some time, but it would only make sense to allow the provinces, if necessary, industrial components and municipal government or associations that have a concern about the legislation to have the opportunity to state their views before the committee in an official capacity.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I should like to compliment the Minister of Transport for introducing the bill early in the session. 1 also want to pay tribute to the dangerous goods branch in the Department of Transport. We are very fortunate in this country to have a branch served by such competent, dedicated and committed people. 1 refer particularly to Mr. Duncan Ellison who worked for many years on this legislation. It has been a very demanding job and I think he tried to accommodate all the views put forward in a manner which is consistent with the theme of the legislation. Taking into consideration the complexity of the bill and its legal ramifications, I think the department and indeed the nation is well served by Mr. Ellison and his colleagues, and I want to compliment them at this time.
I should also like to assure the minister that we on this side of the House will co-operate to see that the bill proceeds. We will want to deal with the various clauses and hope we can receive testimony from witnesses at the committee hearings,


May 2, 1980

but it is not our intention to delay unduly its passage; rather, it is our intention to ensure we have the most effective and workable piece of legislation that is possible in order to satisfy a very important need.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to add my approval of this bill being brought before the House so early in the session. In principle, our party approves of the bill which is entitled the transportation of dangerous goods act. As the previous speaker indicated on behalf of his party, and as I might indicate on behalf of this party, we will not unduly delay its passage.
I do feel constrained, however, to correct the record because of the distorted recollections of the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) regarding what went on last fall. As one who participated in that process and represented my party on the transportation committee when the bill came before it, I must point out that at that time we requested from the then minister of transport no more than the hon. member for Vegreville has indicated he wants from the present Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin)-that witnesses be called and questioned on various aspects of the legislation. It certainly was not our intention then, and it is not our intention now, to delay passage of the bill.
If anyone was acting in a politically opportunistic way last fall, it was the Progressive Conservative government. In response to the Mississauga event, they created the impression that the transportation of dangerous goods legislation was a panacea for the kind of anxiety that was created in the public mind as a result of that event. They pretended to bring forward legislation that they had intended to bring forward anyway as a very fast response to the Mississauga event. In fact, it had been on the order paper of the previous Liberal government and was something that the New Democratic Party had brought up before the Mississauga incident.
In my first question in this House I asked the then minister of the environment when he intended to bring forward legislation on the transportation of dangerous goods. That was exactly one month before the Mississauga event. The minister of the day replied "Yes, and soon." Mr. Speaker, that was my first lesson in how to put a question and how not to be put off with short answers. I learned how to get in my supplementar-ies.
The fact is that the government intended to bring the legislation forward in any case, and for the hon. member for Vegreville to say his party was responding to the Mississauga event was a distortion of history.

Bill C-18 is basically the same bill as was Bill C-25 in the
last Parliament. There are some changes which it is important
Transportation of Dangerous Goods to note for the benefit of the record. For instance, in the new bill there are more ways to defend a charge that a person has contravened safety regulations. Under the new bill a person must establish only that he acted in good faith and took reasonable measures. Under the old bill he had also to prove that his contravention of regulation was not caused by his acts or omissions.
Another change is that when property seized by an inspector is essential to the livelihood of the person who wanted it returned that is no longer one of the reasons for it to be returned. This comes under subsection 15(4).
Under the old bill there was a duty to report an accident or incident that results in a discharge, emission or escape of dangerous goods. Under the new bill there is a duty to report a discharge, emission or escape of dangerous goods. This is an improvement because it broadens the scope with which the bill may be brought to bear on dangerous products.
Under the old bill the government could recover costs of emergency action from a person unless he established that he complied with the regulations. Under the new bill the government could recover costs unless he established on balance of probabilities that he and others for whom he is responsible complied with the regulations.
Under the old bill inspectors did not have the power to seize or remove dangerous goods if there was imminent danger to the environment. Under the new bill they have that power. The new bill does not, however, restore the power of the minister to hold an inquiry if a discharge, emission or escape of dangerous goods results in damage or danger to the environment. It is in this area that we may offer some amendments in committee to restore the environment as a reason for the minister to be able to hold an inquiry. In our view, damage to the environment should be regarded equally as serious as damage to life, health or property.
Two new powers of making regulations are given to the governor in council. First, that of prescribing circumstances in which the handling, offering for transport or transporting of dangerous goods is prohibited; and second, that of specifying dangerous goods that shall not be handled, offered or transported in any circumstances. This should give the power to make regulations affecting modal safety in addition to labelling. In the past, however, the government has not had the will to get tough with the railways and there is not much reason for hope in this area.
These are some of the provisions in the bill before the House which were not contained in Bill C-25 as introduced by the last Progressive Conservative government-and one hopes it was the last Progressive Conservative government.
