speechtext:
Yes, regressive Conservative government. It is important to clear up some of the false expectations that have been created in expectation of passage of this legislation. There is a public anxiety about the transportation of dangerous products as a result of the Mississauga event and the subsequent derailment in MacGregor, Manitoba.
It is important to clear up false expectations about this legislation. Not that the legislation is bad in and of itself; indeed as we have already said, it is good legislation in that it harmonizes and integrates what was once a rather piecemeal approach to the regulation of dangerous goods. In so far as its intentions are concerned, this is a good bill.
I have said what the bill will accomplish, Mr. Speaker, but I think that it is important to put on the record what it will not accomplish. I have read far too many newspaper articles and editorials over the last several months, particularly since the MacGregor spill in Manitoba, which call for the speedy passage of this legislation, in a way that suggested that the passage of this legislation would somehow prevent rail disasters such as that at Mississauga or MacGregor. This is an illusion that must be dispelled.
As I said before, the legislation in itself is a good thing, but it does not pertain, for instance, to rail safety as such, according to Transport Canada officials who appeared before the House of Commons transport committee. This is why I think it is so important to bring this point up. It is the testimony of Transport Canada officials themselves which clears up the expectation that somehow this bill deals with rail safety.
On November 29, 1979, in response to questions posed by myself and by the hon. member for Stormont-Dundas (Mr. Lumley), Transport Canada officials in their answers before the committee indicated that the transportation of dangerous goods legislation had nothing to do with rail safety as such- whether or not cars containing dangerous goods were to have roller bearings, or were to have the traditional friction bearings, or whether the tracks on which the dangerous goods were to be carried were safe and well maintained. This all had to do with regulations that came under the auspices of the Canadian Transport Commission. It had nothing to do with the transportation of dangerous goods bill. From testimony that I have before me, which I will not read into the record but ask members to look it up for themselves, it appears that the only thing the proposed dangerous goods act would change with regard to the Mississauga derailment is that hopefully when firemen arrived at the scene they would know what was in the cars. They would know what had actually spilled in the derailment. This is an improvement not to be taken lightly, but it has nothing to do with whether the derailment would have occurred in the first place. Transport Canada witnesses consistently, when asked about the proposed legislation's effect on the rail safety aspect of the transportation of dangerous goods, said that this question was under the jurisdiction of the Canadian Transport Commission.
This brings me to a second area of concern, and that is the role of the Canadian Transport Commission. Under section 227 of the Railway Act the CTC may make regulations; and under section 296 the railways are required to carry dangerous goods in conformity with the CTC's regulations. Clearly a good deal of responsibility has rested and continues to rest with the Canadian Transport Commission in seeing to it that the public and the employees of the railroads, or for that matter employees of any other mode of transport, are protected.
Along with that responsibility, the Canadian Transport Commission should be given the resources to do the job. For example, the CTC will require more safety inspectors to ensure that its regulations are being adhered to. I admit the hon. member for Vegreville was right on one thing: government restraint was not a creation of the Progressive Conservative government, it was something that started long before when the Liberal party, prior to the election of May 22, began to prove conclusively that it is the second right wing party in Canada. This government restraint had already begun to affect the Canadian Transport Commission. I do not quote my own imagination here; I quote what the president of the Canadian Transport Commission said before the House of Commons transport committee, as follows:
The people we have I think do a pretty good job based on the numbers we have spread across the country, which 1 think is something like 78 (rail safety inspectors), which bothers me. It probably should be 178 instead of 78.
On November 13, 1979, Mr. John Magee, commissioner of the Canadian Transport Commission, testified before the same transport committee that the Treasury Board directed the CTC to reduce its staff even further. The recently published annual report of the Canadian Transport Commission showed an 11.4 per cent reduction in person-years assigned to the work of the commission.
It is a federal responsibility to make best use of existing authority. Therefore, the restraint program as it affects rail safety must be eliminated immediately. In this as in other areas, the public well-being should not be sacrificed to ideological obsessions about government spending. As well, the federal government, through the Minister of Transport, has the power already under section 100 of the Railway Act to apply to the CTC for an order that a railway company constructing a railway which has been aided by a subsidy from the Government of Canada make repairs, additions or improvements to its lines or equipment to promote safety and efficiency. If the company fails to comply with the order, the Crown can put a first lien or mortgage on the railway company for the amount of the subsidy.The power has always existed to promote greater rail safety; it is a power which simply has not been used.
A third area of concern has to do with the fact that railway companies in this country are chartered to render a service to the people of Canada in a safe, efficient manner whether dangerous goods are on board or not; but the railways are carrying more and more freight with fewer and fewer employees. The number of person-hours required to run Canadian railroads decreased 39.5 per cent between 1956 and
May 2, 1980

1975, while the amount of freight carried increased 86.8 per cent during the same period. Between 1976 and 1977, Canadian railways eliminated 60,000 jobs, 31,000 of which were eliminated from road and equipment maintenance, a policy which directly affected safety.
We respectfully suggest that the Canadian Transport Commission be instructed to review the guidelines so that the railways are required to have adequate numbers of maintenance employees for tracks, adequate numbers of employees to do the switching of freight cars and an adequate number of employees to work in all aspects of safety as it pertains to the railroads. In addition to keeping an adequate number of employees, the railways must be required to modernize their plant and equipment. Hotbox detectors should be installed along the heavily travelled main lines. Roller bearings should be installed on all cars carrying dangerous goods. Of course, too, even this will not deal with the problem adequately since the freight car carrying dangerous goods is not always the one that causes the derailment, a fact which points up again the need for general rail safety as a component of safety as it applies to dangerous goods.
The movement of certain dangerous goods may be required in the national interest. Therefore the nation should share the responsibility. Society at large, through its elected officials, should have the right and the responsibility to make decisions about whether particular dangerous goods should move and under what conditions, taking into account all costs and benefits to society, not just the conventional business costs and benefits to a private company.
An appropriate public policy toward dangerous goods shipments must balance the cost of the risk of moving a particular goods with the benefit of having the goods transported. We believe that when it comes to dangerous goods moving in large volumes by rail, the motivation of profit, as the supplier of transportation service, cannot possibly meet the test of balancing all costs and benefits to society.
We support social ownership of railways and the public ownership of Canadian Pacific, because we support the principle of integration of the entire transportation system; that railway transportation not only be perceived as but truly be an instrument of national policy directed toward national unity and economic development. The NDP insist that rail transport receive the massive long-term investment it needs to purchase equipment, improve roadbeds and electrify major heavy traffic sections of transport corridors. 1 say this in order that the headline from a Winnipeg newspaper I read recently which said that the eighties belong to the railways may become a reality, instead of a dream in this energy crisis situation in which we find ourselves.
Crown corporations like VIA Rail should become an instrument through which there can be a restoration of passenger service in this country, instead of a Crown corporation supervising the demise of same. Crown corporations have a role not only to ensure economic benefits to the public, but to ensure that economic development happens in a human and environmentally sound way, free as they are-although I know it
Transportation of Dangerous Goods
bothers my colleagues to the right-from strict profit considerations.
While we are convinced that an accountable, publicly spirited management of our railways would significantly improve railway safety, it would be naive to think that railway accidents involving dangerous goods can be totally eliminated. Accidents on the railways will occur from time to time.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO IMPROVE PUBLIC SAFETY
speechtext: And trucks.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO IMPROVE PUBLIC SAFETY
speechtext:
Accidents will occur from time to time with trucks, airplanes and all manner of transport.
One of the things I regret about the focus which has been placed on the whole issue of the transportation of dangerous goods is that so much has been said about rail transport as a result of the Mississauga event. Sometimes it appears we have completely forgotten that dangerous goods are transported in planes, trucks, boats, and other modes of transportation that 1 leave to the imagination of hon. members. Therefore, it is not just rail safety which is at stake here. However, it is important to concentrate on it today because it is rail safety that is in the mind of the public as a result of the events at Mississauga and MacGregor. The best way to reduce the frequency and severity of these accidents is to reduce the amount of hazardous substances being transported. To do this, we must address the question of our dependence on non-renewable resources, which is my final concern.
We must consider the non-transportation solutions, such as reducing our dependence on non-renewable resources and changing our lifestyles accordingly. Too often we seek as a civilization, never mind just here in Canada, only technological solutions to technological problems, thus compounding our problems by refusing to see that certain technologies as such may be the root of a problem. For instance, our traditional sources of fibres and household goods, such as cotton, leather, and wood, have been replaced by synthetic goods and fibre which are extracted from and/or manufactured with the aid of non-renewable dangerous goods. This has created great conveniences in our way of life, and even greater profit for those who had the advantage of owning and marketing these new technologies and goods. But all this has happened at the expense of the environment, of those left out of work by the abandoning of labour-intensive technologies and of upcoming generations whose access to non-renewable resources for those purposes which only particular non-renewable resources can serve will be severely limited.
Consumption and disposal rather than repair and recycling has created a deficit for the future far greater in real terms than anything governments can do by way of deficit spending or borrowing, because non-renewable resources cannot be paid back. We would be far greater served as a country and as a Parliament if my colleagues on my right spent as much time whining about the deficit in non-renewable resources as they do about the deficit of the government when it comes to budget time.

In recent years more and more attention has come to be paid to the environment, both as it pertains to the non-human environment and as it pertains to human health. But we have a long way to go before we mature into a society that wants to know, and does know, the full effects of its way of living on human life and health, and on the rest of creation in and with which we must live. The science of toxicology, and especially of eco-toxicology, is in its embryonic stage. The fact that so very few people in the recent MacGregor spill in Manitoba seemed to know about the carcinogenic qualities of vinyl chloride, and the confusion which prevailed about the best way of dealing with it, cannot be reduced in the final analysis to the abilities or inabilities of those actually involved or to the legislation that was or was not in force at the time.
Society as a whole has been and continues to be guilty of gross negligence in the attention it pays to actual and potential harm being done to human life by dangerous products, whether it be asbestos, PCBs, methylmercury, arsenic or acid rain, or radiation, to mention a few. We must stand up and take note and consider for once that perhaps we should mend our ways and our doings, lest we find that we have sown the wind and reaped the whirlwind in the form of ecological disasters as yet unrealized but maybe only a short time away, given the often exponential evolution of ecological effects.
In the meantime, before we come to our senses about technology and a great many of the things we are up to these days, the federal government has its responsibilities, the Canadian Transport Commission has its responsibilities and the railways have their responsibilities to see to it that dangerous goods which continue to be transported are transported safely, through special measures designed to take into account the existence of these products. And that is how I see this particular bill. But we will only know how good a bill this is when we have had some time to see what the regulations are like, how they are enforced, whether the new bureaucracy that is created under the auspices of this bill has the money to enforce the new regulations, whether there is the political will to make this bill work. We will only know that as time passes.
However, it is a step in the right direction. In the meantime, as I said before, the government, the Canadian Transport Commission and the railways have a responsibility to ensure that the general context of safety, whether it pertains to rail, air, or marine transportation, is improved so that we do not have derailments and the like in the first place.

I think not. For example, in our riding of Vancouver East there have been several situations where trucks carrying dangerous products have overturned on roads. There have been explosive and potentially very dangerous situations, requiring evacuation of our citizens.
The roads to the port are extremely dangerous. The planning-or lack of planning-of the federal government has never accommodated the development of a Vanterm on our waterfront. I have driven the roads on our waterfront, and workers in that area have pointed out to me that terminal trucks getting out of the waterfront area must pull up over railway tracks at intersections. Nothing is being done to develop proper access to our port areas. There are very dangerous situations.
We also have a convergence of both aeroplanes and ships coming into our port. There have been major incidents in the past which have been very serious. Ships carrying explosives have gone into our port threatening three, if not four, very important and densely populated ridings.
1 know my colleagues will be speaking at length about the problems regarding rail transportation. In my riding of Vancouver East there have been several situations where there have been runaway cars. In one case there were explosive materials, and voluntary evacuation of the area was required. 1 stress "voluntary", because there appears to be no one authority responsible for the over-all co-ordination of safety regulations in this area. This situation at the port of Vancouver, which involves four major ridings, is not peculiar just to the west coast. I am sure it also affects other similar waterfront areas across our country.
What authority will this bill provide municipalities and other levels of government to enforce safety regulations? For
May 2, 1980

example, I am told by the Vancouver fire department that there is no advance warning to them about dangerous commodities which are going to be transported by CP or CN. Can you believe, Mr. Speaker-I hope the minister is listening- that the fire department in Vancouver receives notification of dangerous goods having been shipped through this area one week after the dangerous goods have passed through? I really do not know what this bill will do to prevent major catastrophes.
We also know there is no co-ordination with fire boats. In fact there is only one fire boat in the port of Vancouver, and it belongs to the city of Vancouver. This boat is no longer available to other municipalities, and it should be the responsibility of the federal government under the National Harbours Board and the Canadian Transport Commission.
There are many problems facing areas like the port of Vancouver. Those problems must be raised at this time, and hopefully the matter will be clarified as much as possible during debate on this bill. The Mississauga evacuation and near disaster served as a warning to all of us. It can happen again. In fact there are statistical projections to show that it will happen again, and I wish the Progressive Conservative members from the areas surrounding the port of Vancouver were here today.
The quality and nature of hazardous goods shipped into and through Vancouver are considerable and diverse. It is not unusual to see trains transporting combinations of liquid propane, chlorine, and fertilizer, tripling the danger of explosion. We know that a typical liquid propane tanker has a capacity of about 34,000 gallons. The fire department tells us that the danger of a BLEVE, as it is called in technical terms-boiling liquid expanding vapour explosion-which is associated with such tankers, now being transported along the Vancouver waterfront, is considerable. The danger zone for a BLEVE is considered to be 3,000 feet, or about ten city blocks. Approximately 20,000 people in the city of Vancouver, not to mention the surrounding district, would then be in danger of a major explosion on our railway tracks or in our port. It is no wonder we are concerned.

Transportation of Dangerous Goods
There is no co-ordination and no contingency plan in this area to deal with emergencies. In fact the truth is that no one is in charge. There is a morass of conflicting jurisdictions involving four levels of government, a variety of government agencies and transportation companies. We feel that the CTC must take the lead, although other jurisdictions, and particularly municipalities, are essential in developing an over-all safety plan.
From consultation with the sources which 1 mentioned in the Vancouver area-I hope the minister is aware of this-it appears that the only solution is to establish a transportation safety authority with leadership from the federal government but which will involve all jurisdictions and all methods of transportation. Such an authority would develop contingency plans to deal with the emergency, would pool the resources and divide the responsibilities of governments. It would employ inspectors, the number of whom will be increased under this bill, to enforce safety regulations. Workers should be trained, particularly workers on the waterfront. Truck routes for the transportation of hazardous materials must be studied and designated by such an authority. There must be liaison among everyone concerned with the transportation of dangerous goods.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to rise and take part in this debate. I think it is important for those of us from the rural parts of the country to have a say in what goes on in the movement of dangerous goods around the country. In my riding of Portgage-Marquette in central Manitoba there are over 200 miles of main CN and CP rail line that run through the constituency, and it is on the main lines that goods are transported. I think it is important that we not only think about the movement of dangerous goods relative to the problems that are caused in moving them through large urban centres but that we also think about the transportation of dangerous goods as it relates to movement throughout the country.
I am glad to see that this bill includes provisions to look after many aspects of the movement of dangerous goods, from the way they are packaged and handled before they are transported to the type of containers in which they are moved. I should like to make reference to this later, relative to the train wreck we had at MacGregor last March and the problem we had with vinyl chloride.
It is very important that these regulations not be so all encompassing and involved that they lack common sense, because the most important thing we must have in terms of enforcing them, contrary to what some of my friends to my left would like to think-they would like to regulate everything into the ground-is that they be practical. You must have a

May 2, 1980
Transportation of Dangerous Goods
certain degree of common sense associated with them or they will not work. If you do not have good will, the best intentions in the world will not work. 1 think it is important, with as complex a bill as this is, that the regulations be workable.
I agree with what the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) said, that it was a breakthrough when the regulations were being examined by the committee. 1 was part of that committee and I think it was a very important step. The regulations are so large and there are so many of them that it is important that we have a chance to look at them. I hope the minister will proceed in the same way as the former minister in our government did with regard to letting us look at the regulations when they get to committee.
I hope the minister is serious when he says that he will make the movement of dangerous goods a priority. 1 hope that he does, and I hope that this bill will contribute to making the movement of dangerous goods a little safer throughout the country.
I would like to refer to something that was said in the last Parliament by the member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy), when he said that the minister will have to use the leverage, influence, and power of the government to bring the railroads into line to co-operate in changing the formulas and equations by which the whole relocation process is being administered in this country. It is fine to relocate rail lines around major centres but, as we found out at MacGregor, people live throughout the country and there are problems no matter where you move the rails. Simply moving the rails will not necessarily deal with all the problems.
The main thing we have to think about is that when we do move goods we should take every precaution we can, not only in the movement but in the way that they are packaged to ensure that they reach their destination in good condition. My constituency is a large rural riding and the problems are just as important to us. The fact that some people live in smaller centres does not mean that they would be less concerned about the safety of their families and their communities than people in the larger urban centres, so I am a little upset when I hear people talking about the movement of dangerous goods in cities only. People live throughout this country, and everyone is important.
We had an experience at MacGregor which, although it did not turn out to be as serious as the one at Mississauga, potentially had as many problems associated with it. It involved the derailment of something like 12 tanker cars of vinyl chloride back on March 10. I had a chance to visit the site of the wreck twice and to see some of the clean up procedures that were undertaken. The problem there was how to handle communications relating to the chemical that was spilled, the amount that was spilled, and the associated hazard after the derailment. The wreck took place on a Sunday at approximately 1.30 a.m. A week later there was still a lot of concern in the town of MacGregor as to what had actually spilled, how much had spilled, and the kinds of problems that vinyl chloride would cause in that area. I found this to be extremely disturbing. I think we learned a lot of things from
that, and I think that if it happened again we could do things better.
I was interested to hear my friend from Manitoba, the hon. member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie), say that it was the responsibility of everybody to ensure we have the proper communication. I would like to suggest that if you look at the behaviour of his party in the provincial legislature in Manitoba you will find that it was anything but responsible in terms of ensuring that the public was kept properly and fully informed of the hazards.

speechtext:
I would like to see people check the records on that because I am sure the records will bear me out.
One of the things that I learned from the wreck is that there should be better labelling on some of the cars that move dangerous chemicals. When I had the chance to visit the site, I found a small tag, approximately six inches square, which said that dangerous chemicals were being carried. 1 would see nothing wrong with having something a lot more visible so that, if computers break down, communications are set up to get information to the people involved in cleaning up the wreck. They would not have to rely on this; they could simply visit the site and take a look at the labelling on the containers. They would know from that the kind of chemical that is in the cars that are having the problem.
I am glad to see the minister in the House as I would like to refer to a letter I wrote him on March 20 regarding the inquiry into the wreck at MacGregor. In that letter I suggested that it would be appropriate for the Grange commission set up by the former minister to take a look at the wreck at MacGregor and that I thought we could learn something of the way the communications were handled and from the fact that the people in the town of MacGregor were kept in the dark for too long. I received a reply from the minister just this week in which he pointed out that the CTC was holding hearings at present. I am well aware of that, and in fact I attended the first day of hearings they had in Winnipeg two weeks ago.
I know some of the commissioners personally, I know they will do a good job. It will be a long inquiry. I am sure they will come up with some answers as to what caused the wreck, but I would like to suggest that the Grange inquiry would also be an appropriate vehicle to look at this. Simply because the wreck happened in a place where there were rural residents does not make it any less important than it would be in the town of
May 2, 1980

Mississauga. 1 would hate to see the minister using that as an excuse for not suggesting to Justice Grange that he go to . MacGregor and hold some hearings there. If the vinyl chloride spill had occurred in an area with a larger population, probably more pressure would have been put on and it might have been easier for the minister to see fit to recommend to the justice that he hold some inquiries into the MacGregor spill.
Also I should like to suggest to the minister that the terms of reference are more than broad enough to cover the situation at MacGregor. I should like to refer to the last point in the terms of reference, which reads as follows:
Within the existing jurisdictional and constitutional framework how best co-ordination and co-operation between the various agencies and jurisdictions involved can be assured in the investigative and corrective action required immediately following a rail accident involving dangerous goods. This is not intended to include matters such as the evacuation of residents at large and other related matters falling clearly within provincial jurisdiction.
I think it would be more than appropriate for the justice to go to MacGregor to hold some type of hearing there in order to learn from the people of MacGregor what some of their concerns were, and, if they had an opportunity to go through such an experience again, how they could be better served by the type of actions that were taken.
One of the problems I have with the CTC, despite the fact that I had every confidence in the commissioners, is the fact that the CTC itself is involved in accidents of that sort. When 1 was at the site I had a chance to talk to a CTC representative, a very capable gentleman. He informed me that he had been on the site since the time the accident happened. I think we have a certain element here of the CTC investigating itself. By having Justice Grange look into this kind of an accident, 1 think he would remove completely the possibility of someone saying that the CTC will investigate itself. I urge the minister to take a serious look at carrying out the suggestion I have just made.
I do not want to prolong the debate any longer than necessary because 1 think it is a very important piece of legislation. The sooner we can get to committee with it the better. I think we should look at the necessity of moving dangerous goods in this country. Today I heard a figure which indicated that something like 3,000 goods are classed as dangerous goods that we move in this country. With the kind of lifestyle we have, obviously we will produce things that are hazardous in one form or another either to ourselves or to the environment. But in the case of vinyl chloride and the experience at MacGregor, 1 think the vinyl chloride as a monomer is a potentially hazardous chemical. It has very strong explosive characteristics. The major concern at the MacGregor wreck was at the time of the accident when there could have been a large explosion. But it is also true that in large doses it is a carcinogenic chemical and it has a record of causing certain types of cancer if people are exposed to it over a prolonged period of time, or if the exposure is very large over a short period of time.
Transportation of Dangerous Goods
In this case the chemical is made in Fort Saskatchewan near Edmonton. It is moved to Sarnia where it is polymerized. When it is polymerized, it is made into things which are commonly used. It then becomes a polymer of vinyl chloride which is used in garden hoses and various plastics associated with the wire industry. It becomes a very harmless chemical, and I suspect that all of us come into contact with that chemical on a daily basis.
When we talk about moving certain chemicals, I think it may be well worth our while to see if we could organize ourselves in this country so that we could make use of those chemicals before they are moved, so that when we move the end product from those chemicals there is in fact no danger to the public. I think an industrial strategy or some kind of awareness of that before the fact would go a long way toward eliminating the necessity to move these kinds of goods. In this case it is too late. The facilities for polymerizing the monomer vinyl chloride are located at Sarnia. It must be moved there in order to be manufactured into things that we use every day.

speechtext:
Also the hon. member should be aware that it was not only the members of the House of Commons who brought about the defeat of the Conservative government, but the electorate on February 18 justified the stand of the opposition parties.

May 2, 1980
Transportation of Dangerous Goods
The bill before us has a particular interest in my riding of Nanaimo-Alberni. In that riding and surrounding areas there are three major pulp mills which involve the use of chlorine and sulphur dioxide gases, as well as the use of caustic soda. There is a chemical plant in that area which results in chemicals going through our community, many of which we are not aware of as citizens. The community was concerned. It was concerned before the occurrence of Mississauga. Certainly that was the focal point of community involvement and discussion within those communities as to what types of emergency procedures we had in our riding in order to meet the demands of an emergency such as the one at Mississauga.
At the meeting held in conjunction with the Canadian Transport Commission, there were represented municipal councillors, mayors, regional board directors, union representatives from two major pulp mill unions in British Columbia, and we had industry in the form of a representative of the largest forest products company in British Columbia, MacMillan Bloedel. Also we had firemen, fire chiefs, and emergency planning co-ordinators. Not only did we have the support and co-operation of the Canadian Transport Commission in our inquiry, but also we had public support.
In introducing the bill before us today, the minister said that there is a danger we may have too high expectations of it and of what it may do for commodities transported on rail, on sea and in the air, by cars, trucks and other means of transportation. But 1 should like to tell the minister that the public has high expectations of this bill. The public in my riding has high expectations. People are expecting that this bill will address itself to rail transportation in particular.
Rail transportation on Vancouver Island does not have a good record. There was an attempt by the CPR to curtail passenger service. There was an attempt by the CPR to downgrade or let their railway tracks be downgraded so that indeed they could not have passenger service. Usage had to be curtailed until the CTC demanded that they replace the trestles. The record of that railway on Vancouver Island is very poor. Four derailments within a matter of two months brought to a head the concerns of that community.
I would like to talk about Port Alberni, a major lumber producing town that has a major pulp mill. I would like to discuss the geographical location of that town to indicate the real concerns which the people of Port Alberni feel about railway transportation, the health of that transportation system in their area, and about this bill. Port Alberni is completely surrounded, with the exception of a small valley or inlet on the west coast. There are periods of climatic weather inversions, which means that the air stagnates within the valley. Because it is located on the west coast there is fog, and there is also pollution from the pulp mill, all of which hangs in the valley.
Our concern is that if Port Alberni is put on that railway
transportation system, a derailment coming into the valley
resulting in the giving off of chlorine or sulphur dioxide gas could mean that the fumes will remain in the valley and cause irreparable damage to human health and human life. It is a distinct possibility if one looks at the railway transportation system coming into that valley and the regulations which govern the transportation of dangerous goods on that rail link.
In introducing the bill today, the minister also indicated that we could not expect a great many more inspectors because the bureaucracy required for enough inspectors to ensure safety in our communities would be too costly. We all share a concern about how many people the minister intends to hire to fulfil the jobs which this bill will create. However, there is a need to look at how many inspectors we have today on the railway transportation system. I am not very confident when I look at the minister's estimates for fiscal year 1980-81 in comparison to fiscal year 1979-80, which is the estimates that were recently tabled in the House.
Under the CTC allocation for personnel, we see a reduction of 99 person-years from 1979-80 to 1980-81. Under regulation and control there are 47 fewer person-years and under railway safety, which has already been mentioned today, there is a reduction of five person-years, from 105 to 100 person-years. My colleague, the hon. member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie), said earlier that the CTC chairman had indicated that there are only 78 railway inspectors in Canada. In British Columbia, as my colleague, the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mrs. Mitchell), has indicated, there is only one inspector for all accidents in that province. There is also the question as to whether we even have that one inspector or whether they are about to hire an inspector.
The same kind of situation can be seen with regard to equipment operators. It is important that we have these inspectors. If one looks at the description of what railway safety means and what it involves, one gets a good idea. I think it is important that we understand why these inspectors are needed, so I would like to quote their duties as they are outlined under the railway safety regulations. It reads:
Development of regulations, standards and procedures respecting rolling stock, apparatus, appliances, signals, methods, devices, structures and works used by railways; monitoring inspection and enforcement to ensure effective application of legislation, regulations, standards and procedures in respect of operations, maintenance and construction of railway equipment and facilities-
I will not quote the whole section, but that is the essence of this bill. If the people are not there to enforce and implement what we hope to develop in regulations through this bill, then it has no point. When the minister says that we cannot expect a significant increase, or even an increase, in the number of inspectors, then I think he should re-assess the inspector situation under the CTC. Inspectors are in short supply, and with this umbrella bill there will not be the protection which the people of Canada expect.
We have high expectations for this bill, expectations that one can gain from the provincial and municipal governments, and other agencies, the co-operation which the minister is asking for today. The co-operation within my riding, and I am sure that it is shared throughout Canada, between municipal governments, fire departments, emergency agencies and others
May 2, 1980

in that community has been amply demonstrated. The Minister of Transport is responsible for involving the official agencies-provincial governments, municipal governments and industries-which he has mentioned.
There is a public concern and a public willingness to contribute to the discussion of this matter and to have an opportunity to provide input into the regulations under discussion while this bill is in committee, and also into the changes to those regulations in future years. I am pleased to be able to support the principles of this bill. I hope to participate in committee and give suggestions which I will gather from my riding and which, I hope, will form part of the regulations.
There are a number of things about which we are concerned. We feel the emergency planning activities which go with dangerous cargo and railway safety are not given adequate recognition in this bill. While in committee we will be making further representations about railway safety. As many hon. members know, there are no rail safety standards in Canada. In the case of the E & N Railway on Vancouver Island, safety standards as they apply to the protection of the public on the railway system, are applied in cases where the railway inspector feels that the system is not safe at the speeds at which the trains are travelling and the loads which they are carrying, and they take the form of reducing the speed of the train.
If we do not demand upgrading of our track beds in Canada the ultimate effect of that policy will be that trains will grind to a halt. In fact Canadian trains have already ground to a halt in certain incidents because of that policy. The commitment of our party is to see that this bill does not grind to a halt, but that it is implemented with the necessary changes to protect the Canadian public.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to participate in the debate on this bill, an act to promote public safety in the transportation of dangerous goods. 1 have worked for railways in the area of transportation for 30 years, and I have a few comments which I would like to make. I want to commend the minister for bringing forward this bill, but within it I can see some very serious shortcomings.
There was one drastic accident in Mississauga, and the trade unions and other groups have been investigating that accident. To my knowledge they are still investigating the accident. It disturbs me that those groups who are so concerned about the employees for whom they are working and the various avenues of the whole accident, have not had an opportunity to put forward their ideas with regard to what happened during that accident.
Another area which I would like to discuss deals with the fact that many of our tank cars which haul dangerous goods are not accepted at the interchanges of some of the railways which lead to the United States. If they are not accepted by some of the major railways in the United States, then we
Safe Containers
should take a very serious look at whether, in fact, they are acceptable by our standards.
I am interested in the handling of dangerous material, Mr. Speaker, because I come from a very mountainous area where there are steep grades and curves on the track which handles a lot of dangerous material. I have seen as many as 100 cars having pushers put into the middle of the train-indeed I have seen cases where they could not find a spot to put the pushers in because the material carried was so dangerous. The bill should provide some protection in cases such as that. I think there should be a limit of about 60 cars on trains that handle dangerous material.
Train crews have been cut to two men, one in the caboose and one on the engine with the engineer. The trains come down steep grades, 100 cars or more, carrying dangerous material, and we are here discussing a bill for the protection of people handling dangerous material!
Another matter of concern is that a train could leave Montreal and travel right across Canada, if it had no occasion to pick up an extra car along the way, without a number one brake test. It could go right across Canada without a test, Mr. Speaker. In many places in the United States trains are only permitted to travel a certain number of miles before they must have that number one brake test. I urge the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) to look into this and to see that a mileage limit is imposed on trains handling dangerous material before they must have the number one brake test. If we did that we could make sure that the trains are in perfect condition when they start out to travel across the country.
It has been suggested that the board of transport should have this responsibility. I want to commend the board for its work, but in my experience working on the railway, I came to resent the fact that the board of transport employees would come to inspect facilities and then, if there was a major accident, the same employees would come out to inspect their own work and make a report. I say that is wrong, Mr. Speaker. Some protection must be included in the bill that provides for the safety of not only the workers but of the communities along the route.
In the community of Revelstoke there are level crossings with means of stopping people from crossing the tracks to get to the other side of town. If there were a major accident it would be almost impossible for a fire engine to get to the other side of the train and protect that area of town.
These are all things that must be examined very seriously with the municipalities involved, Mr. Speaker, as well as with other groups. I look forward very much to the meetings of this committee where I hope to have some input, and I am glad to have had the opportunity to speak on the bill.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Transport.

speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of implementing the Hall commission report, including major recommendations, to increase use of ports at Churchill and Prince Rupert, guarantee the Crow rate to the farmer, extend the Crow rate to the processed equivalent of raw materials, pay the railways directly for their losses, make the railways fix up their tracks and buy hopper cars, and give the Canadian Wheat Board more power to control grain movement.
He said: Before getting into the subject of my resolution I wish to apologize to my good friends, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin), the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) and the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Hargrave) in that 1 will not be able to stay to hear their remarks. The parliamentary secretary and I will be making a desperate dash to the airport at about 4.30 p.m. However, 1 am hopeful, and I hope it is not misplaced, that the hon. gentlemen I have just mentioned will be most anxious to support and accept my resolution.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED IMPLEMENTATION OF HALL COMMISSION RECOMMENDATIONS
speechtext:
Some of the Hall commission recommendations have been implemented and worked at by the previous Liberal government and the Conservative government of last year, but there are some other recommendations that still remain to be implemented. As the hon. member for Qu'Ap-pelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) said after the Hall commission report was brought down, it was a Magna Carta for the west. We agree with that. I think people on all sides of this House and from the west, even though they may disagree with some of the minor details in the report, accept it as a package, as a whole. I think that has been agreed upon by people in all walks of life and political faiths.
In the recommendations of Mr. Justice Hall, he said that Churchill should be handling 55 million bushels of grain a year. It still handles only 24 million bushels. Its capacity is not being used to the fullest extent. The hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Murta) made the unfortunate suggestion that Churchill is a luxury we cannot afford, but I was happy to note that other members of the Conservative party disavowed and dissociated themselves from that nonsensical remark. It can save about 1,100 miles in the transportation of grain going to Europe from Saskatoon if it goes through Churchill, but the insurance rates discriminate. This is something which the Ministry of Transport and the government should be examining. These rates are five times those from Montreal. There probably is as much risk and as many mishaps in the marine industry out of Montreal as there ever has been out of Churchill.
The Minister of Transport has, I think, made an effort to try to get the federal government off the hook for some of the money for Prince Rupert. He is finding that it is not working, and from events and statements made in the last week or two it looks as though the government has realized it better not do anything to halt, delay, or renege on commitments made for that port. I am assuming that it is well in hand and going ahead at full speed and that the money will be forthcoming in the full amount from the federal government, and it will not be trying to collect all the costs of the infrastructure, through user charges since infrastructure costs have been subsidized in every other port for decades.
The most important item in the resolution to be considered is Mr. Justice Hall commission's recommendation regarding the statutory rates, or what is commonly called the Crow rate. Mr. Justice Hall not only recommends that the Crow rate be maintained for the grain producers of western Canada, but he also recommends that the principle in the statutory rates be extended to finished and processed agricultural products. This includes other commodities in western Canada, not only grain.
The main reason for the statutory rates is not to provide some kind of handout or subsidy to grain producers for the existence of and the continuing and maintaining of the Crow rate in terms of costs of shipping grain for farmers in western Canada, but to keep us in a position to compete with the other grain exporting nations in the world. For example, the average haul of Canadian grain to the Lakehead or salt water ports is

May 2, 1980
Transportation of Grain
over 900 miles and the next longest haul is in the United States of about 700 miles, but most of that is accessible inland water systems, which are a much cheaper way to move any commodity. Australia and Argentina are among our biggest competitors. They grow about 90 per cent of their grain within a couple of hundred miles of salt water.
The benefits of grain exports bring in anywhere from $1 to $3 billion a year in foreign exchange, which benefits the nation as a whole. Therefore it is only fair and logical that the nation as a whole should share in the cost of getting that grain delivered to our ports.
We are not objecting, and never objected, to the railroads recovering their proven costs of transporting our grain. Mr. Justice Hall said, and this is another aspect of his recommendation, that if grain producers continue to pay the Crow rate, the national government should pay directly to the railroads the difference between the Crow rate and the actual proven costs of moving grain, in other words, the compensatory rate.
I noticed in recent months that the railroads now talk about the commercial rate, not the compensatory rate. That is another little bag of tricks coming from the railroads. The commercial rate on grain from Wakaw to Thunder Bay is something in the order of $3.15 a hundred whereas the compensatory rate-I am guessing but I think I am fairly close-is somewhere in the order of $1 to $1.25 a hundred at the most.
The Minister of Transport says, and he said it when he was in Winnipeg at the beginning of April, that there has been a dramatic shift of western opinion on the Crow. He admitted that the struggle to change the rate will not be easy. Well, he is perfectly right about that. If he thinks that he has ever been in fights before, they will be nothing compared to trying to meddle with the Crow rates. Those who use phrases like "Crow benefit" or "Crow value"-that, in my opinion and in the opinion of many grain producers and farm organizations, is a neat way of destroying the Crow rate that grain producers pay.
The minister and his two predecessors from time to time made reference to trying to get a consensus among the grain industry or farm organizations to the effect that there needs to be significant support from a major part of the agricultural community in the prairie provinces. For a long time, ever since the Hall commission report came down, we have had significant support from a major number of grain producers in western Canada and the most significant and major. farm organizations.
The minister will be well advised to accept the recommendations of Mr. Justice Hall, not only in terms of justice and fair play, but politically. It is called for by the National Farmers' Union, the Saskatchewan Federation of Agriculture which represents something in the order of 25 or 26 different commodity groups in my province, and the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool which represents something in the order of 75,000 grain producers, about as many as there are in Alberta and Manitoba together. They are unanimous on this. That is why I urge the minister to get rid of the obstinancy and stubbornness of his two predecessors on fully implementing the Hall commission recommendations.
I know the minister will have problems with the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) and Treasury Board about the money the federal government would have to pay out, the difference between the Crow and the compensatory rate, but it will not be all new money. We can do away with branch line subsidies, quit buying hopper cars and putting up money to help the railways repair their box cars. Make them do it. It is their job.
The tragedy over the past number of years has been that we have refused, under the law that is now in effect, to make the railroads perform, to the point where the national government, the Canadian Wheat Board, the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta have had no choice but to purchase railway rolling stock, mainly hopper cars.
If Mr. Justice Hall's recommendations are implemented, this will not be all a new or additional cost to the national treasury. The major part of that cost will be made up from money already being paid out in the form of branch line subsidies, railway rolling stock, and the repair of railway cars.
It makes eminent good sense to implement this recommendation of Mr. Justice Hall. I have never been able to understand the reluctance of the two previous administrations to get it done. When you look at who wants the Crow abolished and who wants the Crow benefit or Crow value, when you look at who they are, who they speak for and who they represent, it tells you something. They represent the same kind of reactionary stuff that we had prior to ever having a wheat board. They speak for the private grain trade and the Winnipeg Commodity Exchange.
There are a few organizations on the prairies which agree that the Crow rate should be done away with. Who are they? Who do they represent? A few hundred. Compare that to what the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool speaks for. There can be no doubt that the overwhelming majority of grain producers and, I submit the majority of the public in western Canada, want the Hall commission recommendation implemented and they want it implemented immediately.
The official opposition was waffled on this, as has the governing party. In a campaign bulletin dated April 19 last year, the Conservative party said, and 1 quote:
We have promised that the Crowsnest Pass freight rate be maintained.
After the election we got a different story. The Conservative minister of transport told the UGG convention in Calgary:
I want to assure you that any change in application of the Crow benefit will come only after there is full consultation with producers.
That does not sound to me like maintaining the Crow for grain producers. When confronted in committee, the former minister said:
I want to assure this House that any change in the structure application of the Crow benefit, value or advantage will only come after there is full consultation.


May 2, 1980

That meant that even after consulting it was his intention, and that of his government, to change the structure and application of the Crow rate. If he had said he was changing it in line with the Hall commission recommendation, we and the grain producers would have had no doubt where he and his party stood on the matter. I hope today he will say unequivocally on behalf of his party that they fully support and accept the implementation of Mr. Justice Hall's recommendation as it pertains to the Crow rate.
1 urge this House to accept this resolution. 1 want to say to the minister that, if the House passes the resolution, it is not mandatory but requests him to consider the advisability. It does not say he will do it. I hope he will accept it from the House as an expression of significant opinion, the opinion of not only Mr. Justice Hall but of tens of thousands of grain producers, local governments, the government of Saskatchewan and many rural and urban municipalities in the west which have called for this to be done. I hope members on all sides will accept this resolution and that the minister will go to bat for working on implementing the remaining recommendations of the Hall commission not yet implemented.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I too have to leave in a few minutes for Quebec. This will be my third speech today, although I did not give the one on containers. But I would be remiss if I did not comment on what the hon. member just put on the record.
I am stunned at my lack of decisiveness today! 1 have had great opportunities today which I missed! During the question period there was the possibility to me of deciding on the price of oil. There was the possibility of deciding on improving a tariff on the export of hydroelectric power to the United States. Now there is the possibility of solving all problems pertaining to the grain industry. Here I am without the guts, energy, and the audacity to do it, and I feel frustrated!
We on this side of the House could have agreed to this motion quite easily because the language is simply "should consider the advisability of'. Therefore, one could have done a generous thing for the day, a BA, a bonne action, and approved of that because this motion contains ideas that one should indeed consider.
Some of this I thought had already common acceptance, for example, the "guarantee of the Crow rate for the farmer." I did not think that had to be considered because that guarantee is one of the basic foundations of the existence of Canada. I did not think it had to be looked at again. I am surprised to find it here as a questionable item. I do not think anybody would take it away from western farmers. What could be changed is the formula under which it is handled, but nobody intends to deprive western farmers of this advantage.
With regard to the "increased use of the ports of Churchill and Prince Rupert", I have read about Churchill in recent weeks. I have found that efforts are being made all around. The National Harbours Board is putting a considerable amount of money into dredging the port and improving its
Transportation of Grain
capacity in order to receive larger ships. The railway leading to Churchill is part of the railway rehabilitation system and substantial amounts of money are spent on that. The Canadian Wheat Board pays a lot of attention to that, so I do not think hon. members can say there has been a lack of interest on the part of the Canadian government and institutions in the development of the port of Churchill.
On Prince Rupert the hon. member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) was kind to me today-he has not always been as kind in recent days. My distinguished predecessor might use that as a subject of conversation today if he cares to do so. I have often repeated that what I have been doing there does not deserve the kind of treatment it has been receiving. Even the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) on one of the first days of the present session implied that I was being less of a Canadian than my predecessor was in my approach to Prince Rupert. I was not. I do not think I have to take any advice on how to be a Canadian even from the distinguished Leader of the Opposition, and I do not think my dedication to Quebec or to Ontario or to the west can be questioned.
1 am one of those, and there are many in the House, who can claim that they have an affection for Quebec, for central Canada, an affection for the Atlantic provinces, and an affection for western Canada. So this sort of thing hurts me if I may say so in the intimate mood in which we are operating this afternoon in this chamber. It hurts me because my dedication to the success of Prince Rupert, of the grain terminal port there, is as great as anything I have felt in recent years. I am dedicated to the success of this venture and I do not think I am doing anything which does not make sense.

I worry, too. I do not think I have done anything very different from my distinguished predecessor in this matter. The question of who should build the wharf, the dock, is one which he left unclear. When 1 told the members of the consortium that they would have to compensate on a cost-recovery basis for the expenditure made on it, they were not surprised. 1 did not think I was that cruel or that unfair. I just thought 1 would put some finality to some of the discussions which my predecessor once removed had started. He was in a bit of an expensive mood in some of the communiques he issued but I think he never did say to the consortium that they would get the dock free.
As a matter of fact, if hon. members read the communique of January 31 it is implied-it is even said-that the option was open to the consortium to build the dock itself or to let the National Harbours Board do so. If my distinguished predecessor had offered it free, then obviously there would not have been reference to the possibility of the consortium building it. Elementary, my dear Watson!
I am just saying to western Canadians through you, Mr. Speaker, that the Minister of Transport is rather sympathetic and a Canadian as good as any around here or elsewhere, and consequently he is not trying to "mess up" the Prince Rupert

May 2, 1980
Transportation of Grain
project. On the contrary, he is trying to make sure that it will be a success. So much by way of comment on Prince Rupert.
As to "paying the railway directly for their losses," well, there is discussion on that subject. If one is to convert the Crow rate to Crow "benefit" or Crow "value", I understand there is a great debate going on as to how it should be done- should it be done through the railways, should it be done through the farmers. I understand that intelligent men disagree on how to go about it. This is really the point.
Part of the motion says "Give the Canadian Wheat Board more power to control grain movement." Again, there is a debate on that point and the setting up of a grain transport commissioner is approved by most.
There are different points of view on many items in this motion. This is why, though I have great sympathy with many of the elements of this motion, I find some of them to be of a more debatable nature, and I find the totality to be unacceptable. I just want to say I am not against the resolution systematically.
There is one note on which I wish to end. It has to do with the approach taken to the Crowsnest Pass rate. To an easterner or a central Canadian this is a great challenge. The hon. member who introduced the motion referred to some words 1 have said on this subject. Indeed, in travelling in the west in recent days and listening to representatives of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture and other people, I had the feeling that there is a desire on the part of many people, while defending the Crowsnest rate as an entitlement, to move away from it, having realized that although it has good aspects it has very negative ones also, that it is a double-edged sword preventing, for example, further processing of goods in western Canada.
I have received that impression, talking to people. Coming back to this House after a "holiday" of seven years, and having been the minister responsible for the Wheat Board in 1969, one of the most difficult years in Canadian history-and when things started to go a bit better the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) gave the job to my friend Otto-having come back to this subject now, I had the impression that there was progress because the Crow rate is a right but also a handicap, an impediment to what is considered by most Canadians to be the normal way of running a railway. This is why I thought one of the things I would like to accomplish as Minister of Transport is to begin that debate soon and, hopefully, to begin it in a mood of friendship, in a mood of search for the common good.
These are some of the remarks I wanted to make to the hon. member in answer to his contribution to this debate.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to take part in the debate on this very interesting motion. I certainly accept the apology of the hon. member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin). I know he is probably going out west. I am sure he will read with interest my remarks and we will probably have an opportunity to talk about the motion in more detail over coffee.
I also appreciated the remarks of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin). I think he has clarified, at least in spirit, some of the apprehensions which have been floating around with respect to Prince Rupert. The basic thrust of the motion deals with the implementation of the Hall recommendations and, without patting myself or the previous Conservative government on the back, I think more progress was made in the nine months of our Progressive Conservative government than in any period in total or in part since the Hall report was tabled.
When we look at the specific proposals in the motion dealing with increased utilization of the Port of Churchill, increased utilization of Prince Rupert, the matter of the Crowsnest Pass freight rates, the recognition that the railways need more revenue to support an adequate grain carrying fleet and the necessary infrastructure to do that job and the fact that we need hopper cars and motive power, I think in total we as a government addressed those very important considerations.
I know, and I think I am interpreting the Minister of Transport quite accurately, that in spirit he will attempt to carry on with a number of the proposals and initiatives we have started, and Prince Rupert is clearly one of them. As I have indicated privately and publicly, as long as the Minister of Transport and this government continue to carry out some of the important initiatives which have been started, they will certainly have my support and the support of my colleagues on this side of the House because the matter of grain handling and transportation has been cast aside for far too long. It is a very important element in the exporting of a very major and significant agricultural product, and many steps have to be taken. Some are steps which merely require streamlining and a more effective utilization of our existing facilities. Other steps have to be taken which constitute a major quantum leap in increasing our grain moving and handling capacity to meet the challenges of the eighties and on to the year 2000.
Mr. Speaker, you have been around here for a few years. You have heard talk of Prince Rupert for many, many years, and it has always been recognized as an important component of the grain handling and delivery system. Quite frankly, we have taken the approach that in this country we have four major grain delivery ports, namely, Thunder Bay, Vancouver, Churchill, and Prince Rupert. We need them all. We must utilize them all. Churchill can be utilized to a greater extent, and Prince Rupert certainly can be utilized to a greater extent not only to provide additional capacity but also to provide an alternative outlet when we have the kinds of breakdowns and difficulties we have experienced in the past at the port of Vancouver.
Hon. members know that our government took very positive steps to ensure that the Port of Prince Rupert was going to be developed in a co-operative way. We felt that the federal government had a responsibility because this development was needed not only in the interests of the grain producer and the western Canadian economy, but it was also needed in terms of the over-all national interest of Canada.
May 2, 1980

It was in that spirit that we moved toward putting together a memorandum of understanding at a very early date after assuming office with the consortium, and subsequently called upon and received the co-operation of the provinces and other components of the grain trade to ensure that this facility would be developed. It was in that co-operative spirit that we proceeded. The Minister of Transport and I have had some discussions privately on this matter, and I am pleased that the project is going forward on the basis of the memorandum of understanding and subsequent discussions which took place and that the commencement of construction of this facility will begin, hopefully, this month. I am hoping that that is the target the minister has in mind. Presumably on his venture out to British Columbia along with other cabinet ministers, confirmation of that will be made. I hope that will be the case. We would certainly applaud him and congratulate him on that because it is something that is needed. Unfortunately, in my view the port should be coming onstream today rather than simply being started in so far as construction is concerned.
We undertook to take steps to utilize the Port of Churchill to a greater degree. We were successful in bringing in the MV Arctic to take on a cargo of barley three weeks after the closing of the Port of Churchill. That was a very major breakthrough, which could pave the way for the extension of the shipping season and provide a more all-season port in that northern area.
We also undertook to continue the work of upgrading the rail line. That is something that has to be continued. We undertook to experiment with the utilization of ballast cars, which are owned by the federal government and which lie idle in the winter and are not being used. We undertook to experiment with the utilization of 125 in anticipation that they might very well be effective in carrying grain to the Port of Churchill. So there are those things which have been done.
As a result of the task force findings, we also undertook to increase winter grain movement by rail out of the Port of Thunder Bay. We were able to move something in the order of one million tonnes of grain to east coast ports this winter, and 1 think that is good because it does prove that we can utilize the system we now have in place in a more effective fashion.
The hon. member talked about the Crow rate. I really have difficulty understanding quite clearly what the hon. member is saying, because on one hand he is saying, "Maintain the Crow rate; do not touch a thing".

The hon. member accused me, the present minister and the previous minister, of tampering with the Crow rate, and yet this very motion suggests tampering with the Crow rate. The hon. member says we should extend the Crow rate to processed products and pay the railways directly for the losses. We have been saying that the Crow rate in statute form enshrined in law must remain. We have also said, and the hon. member is now saying it in this motion, that the railways should be adequately compensated for the movement of grain.

speechtext: Right on.
