speechtext:
There is no disagreement on that. Where there is some debate and discussion-and there is no clear consensus, is on how the federal government will pay the difference. That is what is implicit in this motion-how it will be distributed. Will it be paid directly to the railways-that is what this motion suggests-or will it be distributed in some other form? There is not a clear-cut consensus on that point. The hon. member cannot have it both ways. He cannot suggest on one hand the maintenance of the status quo, and recommend change on the other.
The fact that our government, the previous Liberal government and, I suspect, this government, are looking at ways and means of improving is not to suggest that we are going to destroy that fundamental right of western Canadian producers. We have never talked about taking it out of statute form, but it is part and parcel of the NDP game of politics that they spread anxiety and fear amongst producers. I call that a sort of deceitful act on the part of the NDP, and it should not be tolerated by any political party. I think this is a very important issue. We all agree that the statutory freight rate is something very fundamental which should be enshrined in law and continued, but this motion is just one solution, and there have been other solutions proposed.
Surely it is incumbent upon anyone who is a responsible legislator to consider the views of producers at large and, hopefully, to arrive at a consensus which would be acceptable to all concerned. That does not deviate from or subtract from the responsibility of the federal government one iota. The thing is that if we are not going to look at the Crow rate, it means we are going to go on paying the branch line subsidies, buying hopper cars and rehabilitating railways, with the railways claiming losses.
What is suggested is that there might be a better way of handling the whole package, and at this point there does not appear to be a clear consensus regarding a satisfactory package. But the preservation and the enshrinement of the statutory freight rate is fundamental to the western Canadian grain producer. How it is distributed is part of the ongoing debate.
What must be considered is the impact of the freight rate as it applies to the further processing of agricultural products in western Canada. For example, if you look at the movement of rapeseed for export from Lloydminster, Alberta, and Saskatchewan to Vancouver, you find that the freight rate on raw rapeseed which goes to Vancouver and subsequently to the export market is 24.5 cents per hundredweight. If you move it in the form of oil in tankers, the freight rate is $1.03 per hundredweight. If you move it in the form of meal, which moves in the same hopper car as raw rapeseed, it costs $1.08 per hundredweight. So you see that in the application of those freight rates there is a disincentive to process that rapeseed in western Canada, an incentive to market it in its raw form to the market and thereby export jobs as well.

May 2, 1980
Transportation of Grain
1 see the hon. member shaking his head in the negative. If he can rationalize that, I would certainly like to hear it. I simply said that, essentially, the product moves in the same containers and, as a matter of fact, as a result of the CTC findings there is a compensatory rate which has been applied here and subsidies are currently being provided by the federal government as well as some assistance by provincial governments to reduce the differential. However, at present, there is a disincentive to the processing of the product in western Canada.
I believe we must look at agriculture in its total context, not only the production but indeed a further processing of agricultural products so as to broaden our industrial base and thereby to provide jobs to western Canadians. What 1 am saying is that there are no simple answers, as is suggested in this motion. I want to commend the hon. member for bringing forth the motion because this is a debate which should take place.
I hope the debate will take place in a rational and non-emotional fashion because the statutory rate or the Crowsnest Pass freight rate is an emotional subject. However, in the last three or four years, there has been a tendency on the part of producers, producer organizations and other groups, to look at the issue rationally. I think this is a good sign because we all recognize that there is a fundamental principle here. The production and marketing of grain are considered to be important to the nation as a whole-to bring advantages to all of us. I think it is generally agreed that a freight subsidy is required in order for the producers to remain competitive and so as to ensure that they have a fair chance of acquiring the necessary profitability, not only to produce grain for domestic consumption but to produce it for export consumption as well, thereby contributing, as the hon. member for Regina West indicated, toward our balance of payments.
Some of the other actions that were taken by our administration which synchronized with the thrust of this motion are, first, the fact that we tried to establish a spirit of co-operation and confidence within the grain handling and transportation system. It is fair to say that for quite a long time there was much fingerpointing. The farmers blamed the railways, the railways blamed the Wheat Board, and labour was blamed. We tried to bring the components of grain handling and the transportation system together. We brought in the provinces and, as a result, we were able to convince them that they too had a responsibility for this important industry. As a result, Saskatchewan, Alberta, Manitoba, and even the railways, purchased hopper cars. CNR purchased 1,000 hopper cars for grain. The Canadian Pacific placed orders for some 95 locomotives which will be delivered by 1981. The CNR undertook to acquire some 35 locomotives each year.
There is considerable track upgrading, some double tracking, some additional trackage and some new sidings. There has been a co-ordination of grain handling and transportation system as a result of the appointment of Dr. Horner as the grain transportation co-ordinator, and I think the concept of having a co-ordinator has been accepted and endorsed by all parties in the House. There may be different versions of his
terms of reference, but I think appointing a co-ordinator has provided an opportunity to gain better co-ordination and to utilize the system better. It has assisted the Canadian Wheat Board in the task of grain handling and transportation. My discussions with the Canadian Wheat Board have indicated to me that, given the steps that have been taken over the last 12 months, they are now able to go out with a greater degree of confidence and market the grain.
The smooth and efficient functioning of the transportation system enhances the integrity of the Canadian Wheat Board. So far as customers are concerned, confidence is very important. Given the improvements that have been made and that, I am sure, will be continued by the minister, we will be successful in achieving the target of moving 23 million metric tons of grain to export position this year. Perhaps it will be 22.5 tons. We established a fairly ambitious target, but I believe one has to establish ambitious targets in order to achieve that goal. If it is only 22.5 million metric tons, I will certainly not blame the Minister of Transport for the fact that it is half a million tonnes less. The fact is that steps have been taken and I hope he will be able to continue ensuring that those initiatives are taken, because if we can market the grain and move it, I have every confidence that the producers will produce it.
We have established a target and I am sure that this minister and the Minister of State responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board (Senator Argue) have accepted the target of 30 million metric tons for export by 1985 as being realistic. Given the steps that have been taken and the fact that the minister at least implied that he will continue to follow through on these initiatives-I am sure there will be others which will be brought to his attention which, we hope, he can act upon to improve the system and expand its capacity-I am sure we will be able to meet those targets.
I can assure the minister and the House that if we can meet that target, it will not only be healthy for western Canada but healthy for our total economy. Remember that when a farmer grows a bushel of grain he provides jobs in Ontario and throughout the whole country because the farmers' hired hands are working in the factories of Ontario and in other parts of Canada. That is a very important element. When that grain is exported, it provides us with needed foreign exchange and it improves our position as a nation. As the old saying out west goes, when the farmer has money, everybody has money. 1 hope we can continue to work together to improve the system. I do not think we should take rash steps in the short term but we can evolve and make progress in the long term.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, probably it is appropriate that one former minister should follow another former minister. We both came to this House in the famous class of 68. After some three weeks of being elected or participating here in the House, we went to the United Nations and straightened out that august body. I think it took us about two weeks to make that operation work the way we wanted to see it working.
May 2, 1980

I, for one, have returned to the House of Commons, particularly to the private members' hour, after some four or five years. For some years as a minister I did not participate in private members' hour. It was one of the areas which I missed during that particular period.
One item mentioned this afternoon was the fact that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) is a very regular participant in private members' hour. Over some seven years it was my privilege to debate on a very regular basis with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, either agreeing with him in some of the propositions he was putting forward, or in some other instances finding them so expensive that not even he really believed they should have been implemented.
Similarly Mr. Douglas, the then hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands, participated in private members' hour.
I remember when I was in this seat as parliamentary secretary to the minister of finance that the opposition had decided to gang up on a committee of the whole operation. At eight o'clock or 8.01 they had a quorum in the House of Commons and were prepared to vote on a particular motion in a bill. It was my responsibility to stand up as parliamentary secretary waiting for my minister to arrive to speak for some 20 minutes on that particular section of the bill. I well remember Mr. Douglas referring to me as "Horatio at the Bridge". So, there are many pleasant memories one has of private members' hour.
I think this motion is properly drafted. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) indicated that it probably could have been accepted by the government because of its wording indicating that the government should consider the advisability of a particular approach. I commend to any member who contemplates putting a motion in private members' hour that that is the wording which should be used. Quite often there is more possibility of the government accepting that kind of a motion-to study it, to look at it and to implement some of the items suggested-than by simply indicating that the government "shall" and putting that compulsion where it will be impossible for the government to accede to the request.
One of the better things which has happened to the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) is that he served as a minister of the Crown. Although he was a very dynamic member in opposition, I think he is probably better in that role now because he has had the experience of knowing what the demands are in a ministry, particularly in a very difficult portfolio. As one who sat on the outside for almost a year looking on, I would say that he was one of the ministers who had obviously done his homework. He was really dedicated and sincere in trying to make some changes, changes along the lines that he suggested here this afternoon, some of which were implemented by the former Liberal government and some by the Conservative government.
This is a splendid report which Mr. Justice Hall brought forward. We know that it was released in April of 1977. It strongly favoured the extended use of the Port of Churchill. I am pleased that motions such as this and reports such as the
Transportation of Grain
one brought forward by Mr. Justice Hall tend to emphasize that particular approach. Although it will not be used to the extent other areas are used for the export of grain because it may be small in the whole, I do not think it is something that should be ignored. Having lived in that particular area for some two years while working with Canadian Nickel, and later in the Northwest Territories, I know the importance given to that particular port. Something along this line to improve it is something which I think must be looked at very carefully by any government.
The report indicated that the potential of Churchill was to depend upon the continued use of government hopper cars on the Canadian National Railways route, improved marine navigation technology, extended shipping insurance season, continued high performance of the terminal elevator, and the orderly assembly of grain by the Canadian Wheat Board. The commission claimed that Churchill has the potential to handle 55 million to 60 million bushels of grain provided that improvements to rail-those are the magic words, "provided that". Certain things must be done.
Quite often we are looking for instant solutions where there are no instant solutions. Because of the difficulty involved, quite often there is a tendency to abandon the idea that such a conclusion can be reached, given the right spirit, forgetting about some of the political debate which goes on in the House, and recognizing that some of the goals are appropriate. Rather than saying that they should be done tomorrow or the next day, we should recognize that there is a term which must be used or applied when these things can be studied, so that they can be properly implemented and we will not be wasting a lot of money trying to do something in too much of a hurry to appease maybe the demands of people in the area, opposition members or, for that matter, members of the government who want to see particular actions taken.
I think it has been said by all three previous speakers that many of the recommendations contained in the Hall report in fact have been implemented. A great deal has been done by the federal government in support of the Port of Churchill. The National Harbours Board spent almost $16 million on port and port facility improvements between 1968 and 1979. My information is that they plan to spend a further $8 million by 1982. The CN rail line to Churchill is included in the prairie branch line rehabilitation program of the federal government. I am informed that expenditures between 1977 and 1979 approached $13 million, with planned expenditures of $4.9 million this year. This reconstruction work will increase the load-bearing and traffic volume capacity on the line.
I am advised that the Canadian Wheat Board will make the maximum feasible use of the port for grain exports, including co-operating fully with Federal Commerce and Navigation Ltd. for the employment of the MV Arctic in grain service before and after the official Lloyds shipping season. The insurance underwriters obviously are under constant pressure from all interested parties to extend the shipping season, but we realize they cannot be ordered to do so.

The National Harbours Board has sustained an accumulated deficit of some $4.7 million between 1972 and 1978 in the operation of the port. Rather than looking upon that in a negative way, 1 think it is a good investment for something that is very definitely required, not only for the port but also for the export of grain.
I have other items I would like to comment upon regarding this particular motion. I know other members want to speak to this particular debate, so I will close by simply indicating that 1 think it is appropriate the hon. member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) brought forward this particular motion and that he has framed it in the way he has because I think the government must look at all the things suggested in the Hall commission report that are highlighted in a motion such as this.

Mr. Speaker, I should like very much to make a short intervention in this private members' debate. It has been quite a number of years since the hon. member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) and myself came to this institution. I would say that the hon. member for Regina West is highly qualified to make remarks on this subject as he expressed them in his motion. 1 would say his qualifications go back to the days he spent in the CPR many, many years ago at a little town called Richmound, Saskatchewan, even to my own home town of Walsh, Alberta, and to Medicine Hat where we first had the privilege of meeting each other. It goes back quite a long way. But I would say that there is another approach to this very, very complex problem which I want to put before the House this late afternoon. Of course these are personal remarks which refer to the very specific portion of his motion that deals with the guaranteeing of the Crow rate for the farmer and the extension of it to the processed equivalent of raw materials.
1 make no apologies when I say that some of these remarks are a repetition of what I said in the Speech from the Throne
debate on April 18. At that time 1 described them as remarks that were too important for partisan politics. The Crow rate issue is a matter for which it is high time that it come out into the open and be given more discussions.
We are all very familiar with another enormously important debate which is going on in Canada now, and that is the referendum debate in Quebec. 1 would quickly add that the Crow debate presently under way in western Canada is, in its own significant way, every bit as important to western Canada, and I would even say for all of Canada, as is the referendum debate in the province of Quebec. Over the past two years there have been a number of excellent public debates on this issue, all of which have taken place in western Canada at special annual farm meetings or special symposiums called to discuss the subject.
The subject of the Crow rate is now freely discussed with not nearly as much emotion as it was for many, many years. Only in western Canada are these discussions taking place. There has never been a proper debate in this House of Commons or in Parliament on this issue. The closest we have ever come to such a debate was on the PC opposition day of May 26, 1977, when essentially the same subject, the Hall report, was discussed on that day.
